appeal made to them in the, interest of suffering humanity, whether at home qr abroad, goes unanswered. , Before coming out to Australia I had heard a great deal as to the extent of intemperate habits in the colonies. ho far as I have been able to observe in Victoria, there is not here more intemperance than there is in England or in Scotland among the same number of inhabitants. There are too many grog shops. as there are in the old country; but Victoria does not, taken as a whole, appear to require a teetotal crusade any more urgently than Yorkshire or Lancashire. Victoria has its temperance societies and its Rechabite orders flourish- ing just as it has its drinking institutions. I have failed to notice that the latter are more enticing or dangerous than similar institutions elsewhere.

SOME NOTES ON -VICTORIA

No. IV. It is proposed in this letter to refer to some of the charac- teristics and tastes of the Victorians. An opinion has already been expressed that the older colonists and the Australian natives are equally loyal subjects, among the most loyal to be found within the British dominions. The two classes of Victorians, for they are virtually separate classes, are also one in their assertion of pride in respect of, the land in which their lot is cast. The ordinary Vic- torian, whether of the older or younger generation, is clearly of opinion that Australia is a fine place, and that his own colony is the finest. There is no doubt he " blows" about the country and the capacity for doing great things of the people in it—including himself. Whether he dis- tinguishes himself in this regard more than the average New South Welshmen or the Queenslarder I have not been able to satisfy myself, or whether the "blowing" power was stronger when the late Anthony Trollope visite these parts than it is now I cannot say. his I will aver, that to this day Trollops is believed to have considerably exaggerated the failing he condemned. Personally, from my experience of the colony, which has now been pretty varied, I feel cona- pelled to say that the average Victorian "blows" no more than any other ordinary person. I don't think it can be contended that Englishmen are behind hand in "cracking up" the praises of their dear Old Country. Yankees are undeniably ready to declare that the great United States lick the rest of the universe. There are Frenchmen, too, who will be found protesting that the globe has nott,qual to their own charming country. These feelings are all natu- ral, and why should the Australian or the Victorian be found fault with and stigmatised as a "blower" more than them all because he is quick to sound the merits of the fair land he calls his own. The marvellous progress which has been made in Australia, and the brilliant future in store for it, would justify exceptional elation on the part of the colonists, and if this is the case as to the continent gene- rally, it is emphatically the case as regards Victoria, which, though the smallest of the colonies, is the richest and most thickly populated. , While the older colonists here and in the other members of the group have manifested an undoubted preference to model their institutions very much on the lines of the old country, from which they always hear with pleasure and which they hope to revisit some time or other, the "natives" of this colony betray a rather marked impatience of the old world standards. It is here that the distinction and the difference between the old and the new generation are•to be noticed. The early colonisers brolught with them and prac- tised when they got here many time-honoured virtues, such *as reverence for elders and parents and deference to the wishes of others, which are deemed of less importance gene- rally by the race which has sprung up to take their place. A spirit ef independence you expect to find among a people which has had in the early days of its history to conquer nature and to "rough it," as the phrase goes. You look to find this spirit more marked in a country where few men need be poor, and you are not surprised to discover the feel- ing still more pronounced in a colony like Victoria, which in its system of political representation is entirely Demo- cratic. It is hard to understand, however, why this quality of independence should engender, as it would seem to do here, a spirit of indifference for the feelings of others, a spirit which is the parent of self-assertiveness and want of courtesy, and is essentially vulgar, to call it by no worse a name. When you go to a Post-Office window in Melbourne to make an inquiry or purchase some stamps, you must not expect to get attended to in your turn should there be a number there. *Some other person who has coma to the place much later than you will assuredly push himself be- fore you, and look utterly astonished, if it is suggested that he should wait patiently till others who have been longer thau he are served, In the same way yoqs old-faaili9Pc't notions of submitting to what is due o Others, as well as to yourself, would be set at nought at the railway station ticket offices, where the "help yourself" and "elbow your neighbour out" rule is in f 'inswing. The example which isset by the public would appear to be taken to heart by the public servants. A new-comer from the old country will not be at all impressed with the amount of attention he will get from the "assistants" in any shop he may enter or from the employes in any of the public departments. The aforesaid "assist- ants" put on an air of professed indifference as a rule, and comport themselves generally as though they were confer- ring on the customers a mighty obligation by condescend- ing to treat with him. The flippant demeanour of the de- partmental employes, of whom there are many in the colo- nies, would utterly disgust anyone accustomed to the Usually obliging manners of such persons in England. Here in Victoria, where the railways are a State institution,, the railway porter is a Government without being a "civil" 'servant, and so in every branch, and at every turn you find yourself dealing with people who have not and who do wt., apparently care to cultivate the grace of politeness. It is, as I have said, hard to understand wily the spirit of equality which seems to permeate society in this Democratic com- munity should asaert itself in this unpleasant fashion, but so it is, and, being so, it is to be regretted. Flunkey ism, obsequiousness I detest as much as anyone but it is surely not necessary, in order to maintain a manly, independent, and dignified attitude, to rush into the' other extreme. However, when you are in Rome you do as the Itomanl do, and my advice to any, netv churn in Australia would be, "Look after yourself, first of all, and don't too much con- sider anybody else." Ms as a leading public man in Vic- toria said to me before I had been many months in the colony, "It is each one for himself in this part of the world. We don't stand on ceremony." And this "Jack's as good as his master" spirit is attended by one advantage at least. It acts as a discourager of the abominable system of tipping and feeing. Whether it is little or much that the station porter or the hotel servant does for you, he or she expects no "gratuity," and in most cases would refuse it when offered, which it rarely is.

Intimately connected, probably, with the self-reliant dis- position to which reference has been made, is the lack of due reverence for parents and the want of respect for ripened experience characteristic of the colonial born. It follows from this tendency, which has been very properly deplored, and also from the fact that the climate allows of the greater part of the year being sppt out of doors, that the "home tie" is somewhat weak. There is not that strong domesticity which is the spring of so much happiness in the parent land. Under conditions in every way favourable, the young men of Victoria, and of Australia generally, manifest a keen interest in out-door amusements and are proficient in all those exercises which are calculated to develope their phy- sical powers. Indeed, I am not so sure that athletics of various kinds, and notably cricket and football, are not a little overdone. But letting that pass, the breed and the climate and the training have undoubtedly combined to pro- duce in the average Victorian youth a young fellow as active, as enduring, and as plucky as can be found anywhere. In appearance, the colonial born of the male kind do not, as far as I have observed in Victoria, show so well ae the womm. Almost uniformly the Victorian girls are hand- somely proportioned. They are women at 15, and they re- tain their good look's a wonderfully long time considering the exposure by which they are tried. Here, perhaps, some allusion can most flitinely be made -to the dominion of fashion in dress. Feminine adornment in costume is carried to a great height, and this not alone among the wealthy. The wife and daughters of a working man, an artisan, or a clerk are decked out in apparel which in England would be deemed extravagant for their class and means, and a plainly- dressed woman or girl is seldom seen. I cloubt not that far too much thought is given to the question of what to wear among women, elsewhere besides Victoria; but that much expense and anxious deliberation are bestowed on dress here are at once apparent. The climate of Victoria—a gaccession for the most part of bright, sunny days—permits of the re- gular adoption for outdoor clothing of light and elegant fabrics, which in the Old Country would only be brought out to be spoiled or to give the wearer a severe attack of nfluenza ; and the ordinary walking dresses of the Victorian ladies are quite equal to anything seen in Paris or in Lon- don. I am quite sure that no more expensive or more charming examples of the milliner and dressmaker's art could be met with anywhere than are to be noticed any week•day in Collins-street, Melbourne, any race day at Flemington or Caulfield, or at the many picnics which con- stitute so important an element in colonial life. And while there is so much that is attractive about the style and appearance of the average Victorian young lady, I am bound to confess that in manners and conversation too she will compare very favourably with the best of her sex among older communities. She is probably a trifle more addicted to balls and parties, and to being away from home, than is altogether good for her. She resents much parental control, and is undoubtedly inclined to be bold rather than too retirici; ; yet Withal she is a deliihtful per- sen, a.na her vivacious spirits and lively conversation, joined as it is to quick intelligence, make her an admirable corn- -enion, A young fellow with a good income assured, may mely, sprightly damsel such safely tate uat; I. 2° it a burden to pay as I allude to'. To ()ad Who WOold the heavy wages demanded by domestic helps, trio ection would be more difficult. I don't think the general body of Australian born girls take kindly to hiintiehold economy and to household duties. This is most certainly the case as regards the young women belonging to the wage-earning classes, and a proof of this is found in the fact that they will do anything sooner than go out into domest'c service in order to earn their food and fine clothes; and the result of this distaste for "house drudgery" is seen in a great difficulty to get a decent servant at a ridiculously high salary. _ _

When the savings bank returns and the reports of the various friendly, banding, and other thrift societies are of an exceedingly satisfactory character, it would seem a con- tradiction to say that the Victorian working classes are wasteful, and yet, considering the good wages they obtain here, they are certainly not economical. They spend too much money during the numerous holidays there are ob- served in Victoria, and take life altogether too luxuriantly for that. I think they may be said to relish existence 'better than those in a similar grade of society in the Old World. They none of them appear to be oppreslld with much anxiety as to the future. They are truthfElly de- scribed as a light-hearted, without being a specially frivolous race. All classes of the population are undoubtedly given to hospitality, and any sketch of the colonies which did not make mention of this trait, which is no more characteristic of Victorian than of other Australian colonists would in- deed be open to grave censure. The various hospitals and other benevolent institutions in Victoria are, it is true, largely aided from the State Ex- chequer; still private charity. is very active on their behalf, and the money raised by the public as individuals for one good purpose and another is quite equal in the lump to the voluntary exertions of the most generous community. The Victorians are emphatically an open-handed people, and no

The De L'lsle and Dudley Peerage only dates from 1835, but its holder has a right to rank among "Our Old Nobility," as being the representative of one of the most disinguished and popular families in England. te patronymic has become a common Christian name. One of its members has become renowned as the Bayard of England; another has had his memory enshrined in the celebrated toast of the Whig Party, and in one of the most stirring of Campbell's shorter poems. Lord De L'lsle and Dudley not only bears the honoured name of Sidney, but is the owner of the ancestral mansion, around which are clustered so many names dear to poetry and history. The County of Kent can boast of "many an ancient hail," but of none equal in interest to Penshurst. Knole, Leeds Castle, Ightham Moat, must all yield the palm to the mansion of the Sidneys. Bedford and Gloucester; the ill- starrei Stafford-Buekinghams ; the Sidney of Flodden ; the Sidney who was Elizabeth's Lord Deputy in Ireland; Sir Philip and his friend Edmund Spenser; "Sidney's sister, Pembroke's mother," and the Countess of Sussex, who founded Sidney-Sussex College, Cambridge; Waller and his Saeharissa ; and last, not least, that stout Republican, Colonel Algernon Sidney, are all more or less associated with the stately house at Penshurst. The mansion on certain days is open to the inspection of the public; were it not so, the exterior and the village itself would be well worth a visit. I was particularly struck with the air of comfort which seemed to pervade the place, and the good taste with which the nicre modern houses had been erected, in keeping with the stately mansion hard by. Though knowing many of the villages of England, and of Kent in particular, I should find it hard to name one whose exterior is so satisfactory to a stranger's eye as Penshurst. Whether it is, like some others I know, a show village, which has to be considered in contrast with the remainder of the estate, I know not. I simply speak of it as I saw it. The Manor of Penshurst was purchased by the Duke of Bedford, one of the younger sera of Henry IV. This Duke, and the Duke of Gloucester, his brother, who inherited it, both died without issue, and it passed to Henry VI., as next heir. By this monarch it was granted to Stafford, Duke of Buckingham, whose grandson was beheaded by Richard 111. His son succeeded to the estates, but became one of the earliest victims of Henry VIII., when Penshurst , reverted to the Crown. Edward VI. bestowed it on Sir I Ralph Vane; and, after his execution, re-granted it to Sir William Sidney. The Sidneys are a family of Angevin extraction, whose ancestors came over with Henry 11. Sir William, who had been steward of the Household of Henry VIII., and who afterwards was one of the English commanders at Flodden, had a grant from Edward, as an inscription on the house. itself records, of " Pencester, with the manors, lands, anti apprtelnticeS thereto I?el9nging." His inn and heir, Sir I Henry Sidney, who obtained froiu Elizabeth a grant of the advowson of Penshost, was Lord Deputy of Ireland, and played a prominent part in the Irish Wart of her long and eventful reign. Sir Philip, the son of Sir Henry, who fell on the field of Zutphen in the lifetime of his father, was the friend and patron of Spenser; and there is a tradition that the author of "The Faerie Queen" sojourned for a time at Penshurst, and there wrote his early poem, "The Shepherd's Calendar." At Sir Henry's death, his eldest surviving son succeeded him, and was successively created Baron Sidney, Viscount De L'lsle, and Earl of Leicester, by James I. The Earldom of Leicester had been held by , several great families—the Bellamonts, De Montforts, the Dudleys. Elizabeth's Earl of Leicester was the last of the Dudleys who held it; but the wife of Sir Henry Sidney .was the eldest daughter of Dudley, Duke of Northumber- land. The reader will see at Once that, in the modern Peerage, an old title and an old family alliance have been kept in view. The scond Earl of Leicester of the new line was father, beside his successor, of "little Sid for simile renowned," of the patriot Algernon Sidney, and of Dorothy. fflf ter wards Countess of S anderland (the Sacharissa of Waller's poems). In earlier days Ben Jonson, alluding to Sir Philip, had sung of

That taller tree which of a nut was set At his great birth, when all the Muses met. I A. tree, by tlae way, which no longer exists. But we may atilt wander in "the sacred shade" of "the lofty beeches" which Waller immortalised in verse when he vainly paid his court to the prole beauties whom he caP.ed Sacharissa and Araoret. The seventh Earl died apparently without legitimate issue, and left his estates to a natural daughter. The result was prolonged litigation, which was terminated by a com- promise. The daughter in question obtained an allowance, and the estates were divided between the daughters and co-heiresses of the third son of the fourth Earl. The park at Penshurst was then curtailed to less than half its former dimensions. The daughter of one of these ladies was the second wife of Sir Bysshe Shelley, Bart., and she became the owner of Penshurst. Another attempt was made to wrest the estates from the helley-Sidneys. The wife of the seventh Earl of Leicester, from .whom he was never divorced, ;di hough they had long been separated, appears to have had a son, who sought to gain Penshurst by an action at law, but failed. The Shelleys are an ancient Kentish family, whose name is derived from a manor in that county. They formerly held Hall Place in Kent, now the seat of Mr. Samuel Morley, MP. Plan Shelley, who married a Sussex heiress, and who died in 1520, had three sons, from the eldest of whom was descended Sir John Shelley, Bart., who, a few years ago, was one of the members for Westminster. From , the second is descended Sir Percy rthelley of Cm* Goring, I Sussex, and Lord De L'lsle and Dudley. As be ore stated, a Sidney heiress was the second wife of Sir Bysshe Shelley. By his first wife Sir Bysshe had a son, Percy Bysshe Shelley, the poet, whose son by his wife Mary Wollstoncroft Godwin, is the present holder of the baronetage. By his second wife Sir Bysshe had a son, Sir John Shelley Sidney, who inherited the Sidney estates, and whose son was created Lord De L'lsle and Dudley in 1835. It looks as though the peerage was fine to his matrimonial connections, for in 1825 he married Lady Sophia Fitzclarence, and his 'peerage was obtained when his father-in-law was King. Be this as it may, the sternest Republican will hardly complain that the illustrious house of Sidney is still represented in the Peerage of England. As the present Lord ia the son of the Fitzclarence marriage, he can boast not merely that he has Royal blood in his veins, but that he had a King of England for grandfather. Lord De L'lsle and Dudley owns in Kent Yorkshire
Total

The Yorkshire estates appear to have been derived by his marriage with the only, child of the late Sir William Foulis, Baronet, of Ingleby Manor, in Cleveland. The baronetcy was obtained by Sir David Foul's, one of the Scotch favourites of James 1., who became in succession Cofferer to Prince Henry and Prince Charles, and held divers other appointment.. • His emoluments as a courtier enabled him to purchase Ingleby, an ancient baronial seat. In 1633 he became a victim to the tyranny of Strafford, and for speak- ing plainly concerning the illegal exactions of that Minister he was hauled before the Court of Star Chamber, was deprived of all his offices, committed to the Fleet, and fined £5 000 to the King and £3.000 to Strafford. To defray these ruinous fines he was compelled to sell a portion of his estate. The son of Sir David, at the same time, was also committed to the Fleet, and fined £5OO. The subsequent history of the Foulis family has been uneventful. ' The connection of the Sidneys with English history, that is from the day when Sir William fought at Flodden to the day when Algernon died upon the scaffold, only occupies a space of about 170 years; since that time the ancient energy seems to have died out. We might spare, perhaps, the memory of " Flodden's fatal hill," and of the fierce rigour of Lord Deputy Sidney's government of Ireland; but we could ill spare from our national annals the pathetic story of the field of Zutphen, and the stoical fortitude with which Alger- non met a tnt ie gleioua death. At the §aMo time, we cannot forget that it was as courtiers the Sidneys gained their possessions. On the gateway at Pensburst, In the records of the Foulis family, in the date of the modern i-Z"e, the same tact is reaorded. It remains only to be added that Lord Lisle, the defendant in the Brompton County Court case, who is said to have set up his privileges as a Peer when sued for a paltry coal mer- chant's hill, is not in any way related to the Sidneys. He is an Irish peer, whose family name is Lysaght, and whelke ancestors distinguished themselves in the Irish wars of 1641 and 1699. This nobleman is, or rather was, owner of 10,376 acres in the counties of Cork and Tipperary, with a rent-roll of £6,558. A "Friend of the Family" says that he is an upright and honourable man, though the victim of most adverse circumstances, and that, through the extrava- gance of his predecessors and the unavoidable expenses of Chancery, he finds himself, as an old man, penniless, having even sold his life interest in all his property for the benefit of his creditors. lam sorry for his misfortunes, but as he has several grown-up sons he ought not to be left destitute. As for the coal bill, a penny subscription among all the Peers would suffice.

No human being can come into this world without in- creasing or diminishing the sum total of human happiness, not only of the present, but of every subsequent age of humanity. "Can a man marry on ten dollars a week I." was the ques- tion propounded for discussion before the " Young Mena' Economic Benefit Society," and a female auditor shrieked: "Not if his girl knows it I" A. little girl, four or five years old, whose hair is a bright red, was requested one morning by her grandfather, who was about to return to his home in the city after a visit to her parents, to give him a lock of her hair to put in his pocket- book "to take home to grandma." "Why, grandpa," said little Betty, quickly, " it would burn a hole right through your pocket-book before you could get there,"

THE PRINTER'S DEVIL.—XI. [By ANGLO-:..-4coyus.] (Me right of re-publication is reserved.) The few items dealt with in this chapter will, I think, war- rant me in indulging in what may be termed an apologetic digression. Like a good many more Sco,chrnen, I am, and have been, hard to convince as to the truth of some asser- tions and records. When as a boy I read end doubted Nfungo Park's statement, anent beefsteaks being cut from a live bullock, I little reckoned I should meet in manhood
military officers who bad accompanied a British expedition to Abyssinia, and who had seen the cruel practice resorted to with their own eyes. When I read with wonder Hanno's _ _ _
descriptions of the Gorului and hairy people, little din I dream that I should myself ever have the honour or suffer

the indignity of curving two distinct and live gorillas in my arms. I had at one time my doubts about the "accom- modating stomach " of the ostrich, but I had not then had the unique experience of helping to defend a refreshment . . _

bar against the attack of one of the struthio tribe, or of seeing my gloves and umbrella handle disappear down its capacious maw with the same facility as cakes and fruit. I had laughed at accounts of the fondness of Lapps for oleaginous substances, and of their

peculiarly ancient and fish-like smell, but I had not then experienced the peculiar sensation of spendiog half an hour in the same room with half-a- doz m of them, with all their paraphernalia and three live reindeer thrown in. A strong cap of Lewis's tea, laced with a dash of that sixteen-year-old whisky a deservedly and universally respected Newtonian. and old friend of mine, keeps in his cupboard against "emergencies," would have come in handy after or during that experience. But I had perhaps better be careful how I allude to or recommend

. . sedatives, seeing that a demon of the "primrose" order is just now toucbin.. me 'up in the matter of my "luxuries" to the monetary tune represented by the difference between 145. and £2 is. Bd. I bad, at

one time, my doubts about the asserted paucity of costume worn by the natives of tropical climates, but I had not then seen a modern opera-bouffe performed, or had "a private interview with a couple of African princesses dressed in their native costume," to quote the intimation given on the cards of invitation. In our theatres, and ht Our watering- places, the "veneer of civilisation " is certainly being rubbed off. But I hope it will be a long time before we come to the state of "natural manners" described by Mrs. Bridges in her "Travels Round the World." At a fashion- able Japanese watering-place, where the tanks of warm mineral water are open to the street, while writing in her room she observed a lady and her child sitting down to cool on the door-step :—" Neither of them has a scrap of cloth- ing on, only some long tortoise-shell pins in the hair; and now I see she has slipped on her straw sandals, while a gentleman, also unclothed, has coma up to talk to her and hang himself out to dry. It is really very startling at first. Other people are sauntering up and down, as on the pro- menade at Homburg, but seem entirely comfortable with nothing whatever on." Mrs. Bridges might have explained how a person " hangs himself out to dry." Or is the Printer's Devil responsible for the description of the unique attitude alluded to? I knew that a mischievously-inclined or restless bull-calf could be quieted or led for a time by letting it have your hand to suck, but I did not know till ill-luck placed me in the awkward dilemma of finding myself between the two horns of a couple of—to me at all events—too inquisi- tive rhinoceros calves, that they could be quieted or amused in the some way. I had read all about the "patience of the camel," but I had not acquired the practical knowledge that cautious Arsbs guard against the absence—or, it may be, presence —of the ," waiting virtue" by the insertion of a wire through the animal's nose. I used to shake my head over the accounts of the existence of giants and fairer folk, hut I had not thee bad the pleasure of taking, wine with the genial Chang or been kissed by the pretty little Mid- gets. I ali7o confess that Iw is sceptical over Miss Bird's graphic description of the Moos of J-tpin ; but I was con- vinced of the truth of her account when Mr Fermi imvited me to the first private reception Krao held in London, and I saw and felt the soft silky hair with which her body was covered. And if what follows be correct, I presume that Miss Bird's account of the existence of the "tailed -tribe" is in the main correct. I have no wish to joke on such a sub- ject, let alone treat it irreverently; but it is just possible that the "loss of the tails" justified the " robbery of the wings," that Hanno told the truth, auel that the Darwin theory is based on fact. To resume, the New Testament reviser's are said to have discovered a curious misprint. It is asserted that the word " rib," in the sc.c.md chapter of Genesis, us'd in describing the creation of Eve, ought more correctly to be rendered " And again, that the so- called ravens which fed Elijah were not ravens at all, but gipsies. In this connection it may interest readers of The Examiner to know that in the gipsv dialect the word " devel" means " God." Moses, again, has been represented with horns upon his head lay medveval artists, through a mistranslation of the Elebrew word " karan," which in the Vulgate is rendered "cornuta," or horned. What is really meant is rays of light darting out, in the manner In which the sun is repre- sented in the rude woodcuts of early almanacs, &a. It is just possible that a " rude " or imperfect illustration of the I forelock of the horse is accountable for the modern illustra- tions of the unicorn and its horn. I wonder what George Sanger will say to ills! A and K. C. must have had some- thing to do with the niistrauslation of 11. Samuel, viii., 4. Our version says that " David houghal all the chariot horses." There is no such act of cruel!), recorded in the original. The Hebrew " Vayaker David eth col harechab," means "And David disjointed all the chariots." It is, how- ever, stated that he reserved one hundred of the chariots e not the horses for them, as in our version. To cgipe to a case of pure accident in connection with the press, shall never forget the painful and puzzled look of the worthy editor of a religious newspaper and review during the " bad quarter of an hour" he suffered and experienced through the fact that the disappearance of a ketned accent from a Greek letter in a sentence of the same language completely altered its meaning. The omission of an accent in Greek, or its insertion in the wrong place, will in some cases play the deuce with the meaning of a sentence, as it did in the instance alluded to.,

Willie has a four-year-old sister Mary, who complained to mamma that her button shoes were hurting her. "Why, Mettle, you've put them on the wrong feet." Puzzled, and ready to cry, she made answer, " What'll I do, mamma? They's all the feet I've got." CHARGE OF FALSIFYING RETURNS.—Pris ate Montgcmery, Carluke, was ou Thursday committed for trial by the Pro- curator-Fiscar of Midlothian upon a .charge of having falsi- fied returns by means of which he was declared the winner of the Caledonian Challenge Shield at the Edinburgh and Midlothian Association competition in June last. FATAL BATHING ACCIDENTS.—A gentleman named Carl Erik Mautelin, a Swede, met his death while bathing on Saturday at Ty nemouth. In diving in shallowyrater trom a bathing machine he struck his head against the ground and sustained concussion of the brain. He was removed to the Grand Hotel, where he died a short time afterwards.— While three brothers, named Maxey, of London, were bath- ing on Sunday morning at Skegness' Lincolnshire, one of them was seized with cramp and was drowned within a very short distance of his brothers.—On Sunday afternoon one of a party who had come from Preston in a waggonette went into the water to bathe at Naze Point, Lytham. He, how- ever, suddenly disappeared in the presence of his friends, and was drowned. His body was found on Monday. The name of tha deceased was Charles Warner, and he was a moulder. The directors of a new bank which had been established in a town in Indiana had engaged the services of i watchman who came well recommended, but did not seem over-experi- enced. The president, therefore, sent for him to post him up a bit, and began —James;this is your first job of this kind, isn't it ?—Yes, sir.—Your first duty must be to exer- cise vigilance.—Yes, sir.—Be careful how strangers ap- proach you.—l will, sir.—No strargers must be allowed to enter the bank at night under any pretext whatever.—No, sir.—And our cashier—he is a good man, honest, reliable, and trustworthy; but it will be your duty to keep your eye on him.—But it will be hard to watch two men and the bank at the same time, sir.—Two men—how ?—Why, sir, it was only yesterday that the cashier called me in for a talk, 1 and he said you were the squarest man in Indiana, but it would be just as well to keep loth eyes on you, and let the directors know if you hum, around after hours! THE SETTLER AND THE TRAVELLER.—" Holloa," called a traveller, stopping near an "old timer's" ,house, and ad- dressing a man. Have you seen men on horseback passing here? Yes.—Were there four in tile party? Yes! jest PM that.—Where do you suppose they are by this time P &ale o' them dead I reckin.—What! You don't say so! Don't Isuppost tney;ve had any trouble, do you? I reckin they have.—Did they have a fight with somebody? Don't know. --What makes you think some of them an dead? It's time.--I don't understand you. What did yer ax me? If you had seen four men pass here.—An' what did I tell you? That you had. salt what makes you think that some of them are dead? ?Cause it's time.—Still I don't understand you.—What did yer ax me? If you had seen four men pass here.—What'd I tell yer? Oh, hang it! you said that you had.—Wall.—But why do you think that they had trouble? 'cause it's time.—l never met just such another case. declare, I don't understand you.—What did yex ax me-? ' —Blame your foolishness! You know what I asked you. I asked, as plainly as I could speak, if you had seen four men pass here? What did I tell yer ?—I don't believe you've got half sense. You talk like an idiot. You told me that you had. Wall P—l want to know why you think that any of them are dead? 'Cause it's time.—l won't stand any such foolishness. If you don't tell me I'll get down and whale you till you can't stand up.—Get down, then, get down. You'll find me a mightapeart old chap. I've been a waitin' fur you a long time. Mill (calling his son), hold the gen'leman's hose till he gets down an' mixes with your pap.—My friend, I don't want to have any trou- ble; I asked you a simple queetion.—And what did I tell yer 2—Here, boy, hold this horse. No blamed fool shall treat me that way. I'm an Arkansaw man myself. (The boy took hold of the 'bridle reins, and the traveller dis- mounted.) I'll give you one more chance. Have you seen four men pass here? Yes.—When? Wall, now you're gettin' at it. I seed 'em twenty years ago, an' I reckin some o' them are dead by this time. I've seed more than four men pass here in my time.—The travelled reflected for a moment, and asked: Have you seen four men pass here to-day? No, sir.—Why didn't you say so at first? You lasked me if I had seen four men pass here, but you didn't say when. When you ax a man a question, ax him squar'. —The traveller, without replying, mounted his horse and rode away.—Arkansas Traveller.

PERSONAL Lord and Lady Derby will stay for the next month at Fairhill, their place near Tunbridge, after which they will go to Knowsley. The Duke of Westminster has consented .to preside at a meeting to be held shortly at Chester with a view of hi- (lacing the Royal Agricultural Society to hold the show for 1885 in Chester. Before leaving town for his Perthshire seat, Earl' Cairns bought up all the portraits on tale of Miss Fortescut,, the aesess, who is engaged to be married to his lordship's SOti, Viscount Garmoyle. Mr. Jesse Coilinas has given notice to wive- a resolution nest sessions affirming the necessity for local self-govern- ment in Ireland as 3 means of securing permanent peace and contentment in that country. It is understood (says the Daily Telegraph) that the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill will be re-introduced early next session, and dealt with by the House instead of being again referred to a Grand Committee. Str Charles Duke, President of the Board of Trade, has intimated to the Town Council of Paisley his acceptance of their invitation to have the freedom of the burgle con- ferred urn tic Occasion of his visit to that town in October. Tilts atatigeoietits for Mr. hatniamhin's tour of the Brit- ish coast are now complete. He will sail in the Trinity yacht Galatea, and he will visit Plymouth, Bristol,Fal mouth, the Scilly Isles, and ports on the North-West and North- Eastern Coasts. Politicians of all shades will regret to learn that the fatigues of the session have 'somewhat seriously told upon Sir Stafford Northcote. Tue right hon. gentleman has with difficulty been able during the last few weeks to fulfil his parliamentary duties. The Duke and Duchess of Connaught visited Norwich, on Monday afternoon, for the purpose of opening the new baildings of the Norfolk and Norwich Hospital, and to attend a biz mar in aid of the hospital funds. Prince Albert Victor of \Vales also assisted at the opening ceremony. It is understood that on the termination of liks Parliamen- tary duties, the Premier and Mrs. Gladstone will visit Old Colwyn, and take up their residence on the Marine-terrace. Mr. W. H. Gladstone, M.P., and the Hon. Mrs. W. H. Gladstone, with their family, have been residing at the .1 Marine Hotel, Old Colwyn, during the last fortnight, and , not at Colwyn pay, as has been stated.

A conference of the representatives of the Australian colonies will be held shortly on the annexation of New Guinea and other islands in the Pacific. ANTI-LICENSE AGITATION. The inhabitants of Bootle beld a town's meeting on Thursday night, presided over by the Mayor,, and passed resolutions requesting the magis- trates not to grant any fresh licenses for the sale of intoxi- cating liquors. SOCTII WALES UNIVERSITY cOLLEGE.—The committee of the South Wales University College, on Wednesday, de- cided to rent the infirmary buildings at Cardiff for college purposes. Arrangements were also made for opening the college in October. • A DESERTER AT ST. HELENS.—A young wom in dressed in uniform, named John Patrick O'Brien, pleaded guilty at the i St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, to being a deserter from the Ist East York Infantry Regiment. He had, it ap- peared, gone into the police office the previous evening and given himself up. He was remanded to await an escort. EMIGRATION or PAUPER CIIILDREN.—The Guardians of Prescot Union having resolved to send twenty-five chil- dren to Canada, the selected children attended before the magistrates at Prescot, on Wednesday, to signify their a.sent to their emigration. The children, who were brought ffoin Kirkdale Schools in a waggonette, looked well and cheerful. BICYCLING—At. Leicester, on Saturday, F. Lees, of Shef- field, attempted to ride a distance of 20 miles in an hoar. Great interest was taken in the event, a very large number of spectators being present. Lees went off at a very rapid pace, finishing the half distance in 29min. 22secs , and even- tually completed his twentieth mile in 58in1o. 34secs. Daring the remaining portion of the hour he rode half a mile and 25 yards, this being by far the best performancl on record. R. Howell, of Coventry, also did the best mile on record, his time for the half mile being lmin. 20secs., and for the Iruile 2cnin, 40 4-5 secs.

,_ - - --------,..- SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO 'A PRESCOT TRADESIA&N.—A. serious accident hippened on Friday to Mr. Alfred Taylor. son of Mr. Peter Taylor, builder, Prescot. While engaged in pointing a wall at the Prescot Police Office, the plank on which he was standing slipped from one of its supports, and he fell a distance of fifteen feet, alighting on the right side of his head. lie was carried home insensible, and remained unconscious for some hours, having received a very severe and daogerous wound on the head.

DETAILS OF THE MURDER OF CAREY.

Cape newspapers which have reached Plymouth give fall' derails of the assassination of James Carey. Erom these it. appears that before the Melrose left Cape Town a rumour was current that a man who had travelled from London on board Up Finfauns CasVe under the nfttllA of Power, and was proceeding further on board the Melrose, was James Carey, the informer. A steward on board the Kinfauns Castle had pointed out a 'paragraph in a newspaper to. O'Donnell, who shot Carey, stating that the passenger Power was Carey, the informer. O'Donnell on learninz this, showed great excitement, and said that if he ha& known Carey was oa hoard the ship be would have swung for him. O'Donnell, it appears, had only booked to the Cape, but some days before arriving there bad arranged to proceed to Natal, and appeared to he well supplied with money. He had little luggage with bim, bot- in his box a suspieicus-lonhtng else, nine inches square and seven inches deep was fund, and on examination it provcct to be an electric-machine, which the captain of the Melrose thought it prudent to throw overboard, .Several passengers saw the shots discharged at Carey, who died about three- quarters of an hour afterwards. There is nothing to show that O'Donnell knew the passenger called Power was really James Carey until he saw the staternorit to that effect ii. the newspapers, so that the belief that he was specially sent out to " execute " Carey is apparently without foundation. O'Donnell, the murderer of -James Carey, will be sent to. England on September. 4, in order to undergo his trial.

• HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Irish Parliamentary Registration Bill and the Scotch Local Government Bill were thrown out on the triotion for their -second reading. The Corrupt Practices (Suspension of Elections) Bill, the Tramways and Public Companies <lreland) Bill, and the Public Works Loan Bill were read a second time. The Patents for Inventions Bill was read a thitd time and passed. The Education (Scotland) Bill went , through committee. The reports of amendments to the Pau- -1 hamentary Election (Corrupt and Illegal Practices) Bill was reo,ived. The Expiring Laws Continuance Bill passee through committee, as did also the Labourers' (Ireland) Rill. The Cholera Hospitals (Ireland) Bill was read a third time and passed.—The House then adjourned during plea- sure.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnESDAY. NEW WRIT.—A new writ was ordered for Rutland in room of the Right Hon. Gerald Noel, resigned. SUOMI BOUNTIES. In reply to Mr. Morley, Mr. , CEINMBERLAIN said her Majesty's Government did not think Ithat at present any good would be done by making repre- sentations to foreign Governments as to sugar bounties. 1 MADAGASCAR.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied to a number of questions relating to recent events in Madagascar, but his , answers contained no • additional information than he gave In replying to Sir Stafford Northeote's inquiries at the pre- vious sitting. - COURT OF CRIMINAL APPEAL BILL.—Mr. CrLADSTONE announced that the Government had abandoned all hope of being able to proceed with the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill. THE WORK OF TEE SESSION.—On the motion for the second reading of the Appropriation Bill, Sir S. NORTHCOTE criticised the manner in which the Government had ordered 1 the business of the House, and pointed out that out of eleven measures promised in the Queen's speech only two or three were about to pass into law. He referred to the policy of the Government in South Africa, and said that the gloom which hung over South Africa hung in triple darkness over our ralitions with Madagascar. The reti- cence of the Government on that question was an alarming symptom which, unless there was some good maser' for it, was a serious mistake.—Mr. GLADSTONE acknowledged the , right of Sir S. Northcote to review the work of the session, 1 but he did not admit the arithmetic of Sir Safford Northcote as to the measures of the session. Thirteen measures were mentioned in the Queen's Speech,. and of these five had passed the House of Comtnons. Except the London Government Bill, the live bills passed were decidedly more than weighty and important than the eight not passed. Taking the results of the legislative work of the last 50 years, and considering the business did not begin this year till after Easter, he contended that the results of this session went far beyond those of an average year, and the Government could therefore afford to War the small criticisms of hir S. North- ccile. The reason why the House did not pass more legis- lation was that the House was not master of its own busi- ness. What they mast look to for a remedy was the means of action possessed by the House through the medium of the Grand Committees. As to Ireland, he thought the success of the Land Act and of the vigorous administra- tion of Lord Spencer deserved a word of acknowledgment even from the Opposition. With respect to the gloom re- presented as hanging over Madagascar. 1,,s ....octilled that nothing had occurred f, a:.,...,u tue minds of those who set value on the relations between France and England. He believed reticence had nevei been carried so far as in the late Government, and maintained that there was no undue reticence at present. He regretted the inuendoes thrown out as to the policy of the Government in India, and feared they woulel tend to weaken the hands of Lord Ripon. He admitted there was great opposition to the Ilbert Bill, but it was a step the end of which would be the establishment of a degree of harmony between Europeans and natives that in former times was unknown, and they were building up with care • and energy a fabric that would last, and which it would be their hirh privilege to administer.— After some criticisms by Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Mr. Bourke, Lord G. Hamilton Mr. Gorst, and Mr. O'Kelly, the debate was continued by 'Mr. Warton, Mr. A. O'Connor, Captain Aylmer, Mr. Magniac, Mr. Biggar; and Mr. Healy.—The Bill was read a second time. AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS (ENGLAND) BILL.—The House proceeded to the coneideration of the Lords' amendments to the .Agricultural Holdings (England) Bill. The first amendment, extending the proviso as to the inherent capabilities of the soil to the third Rot of the schedule, was accepted by Mr. Dodson on behalf of the Government.—A division was, however', challenged by Mr. BARCIAY, when the amendment was agreed to by 121 votes against 64. The Lords' amendments exempting holdine;s under specific agreements with regal d to compenstion and raising the interest on the sinking fund for drain Age executed by the landlord were disagreed to. Among other amendments of their landships which were disagreed with was one limit- ing the compensation for outlay on manures in the last year of the tenant's occupation of his holding—the majority in this case being 126 to 51. The amendments to this and the Scotch Bill being disposed of, the other orders were run through and the House adjourned.' • HOUSE OF LORDS —WEDNESDAY. A number of bills were read a third tilos and passed, and some others advanced a stage. The consideration of the Commons' amendments to the Lords' amendments to the Agricultural Holdings (England) Bill cAme up for considera- tion. Lord Salisbury refused to recede so far as concerns the clause refusing compensation to the tenant where there had been any condition that the tent should make the im- provements. On a division, there were 48 votes for and against, and the Lold Chancellor de:dared in favour of tit, non-contents, In the resnit, Lod Salisbuty's amendment was carried. On the Scotch Bill a similar proviso was
agreed to.

div.head: THREE PERSONS SHOT BY A BURGLAR.
div.p: THREE PERSONS SHOT BY A BURGLAR.

A. daring attempt at burglary was made on Saturday night at the Nolth London Collegiate School, Holloway, also known as the Hamilton House School for Youno. Ladies. The school is in the occupation of Mr. Hassell, and situated at the corner of Loraine and Annette-roads, Holloway, the front entrance being in the former, while there is a side en- trance in the latter. At abont a quarter-past nine, Mr. Has- sell was sitting on a couch in the dining-room facing the window when he was surprised to see a man endeavouring to effect an entrance. Mr. Hassell sprang from his seat to seize the man, but he was on the alert, and in a moment dropped on to the conservatory roof and slid down into the garden (about six feet), breaking two large panes of glass in his descent. He then leaped the wall into the Annette-road. Mr. Hassell had raised a cry of " Stop thief," and "Murder,". and rtished round to the side of the dieuse. His cries brought several persons to the spot, who started in pursuit of the would-be burglar. Finding several persons does upon him he turned round, pointed a revolver at a woman, 'and fired, wounding her in the shoulder. By this time the men who were following had got very near to the man, and two of them rushed for- ward to seize him. but he turned his revolver upon thena and fired three shots, one of them striking the foremost of the pursuers, named Henry Hurst, of 39, Andover-road, Holloway, in the kneecap. and disabling him. One of the other two shots took effect upon another man named Joseph Kendrick, of 8, Campbell-road, Holloway, the bull, t piercing his ankle. The pursued man then made off in direction of Highbury Vale, and altlionoli east sight of. As he pereone i were still pursuing him he we—eett ran down th e ye-re-ea-toad he was etrrying his boots and a Jemmy "in one hand, and a revolver in the other. Con- .l stables soon arrived, and their attentioti's were addressed to the injured persons, who all live ,within a short distance and were conveyed to their houses. The injured woman, whose name is Loonies, and who lives in Orpingley-road, , Holloway, was found to have a deep flesh wound in the shoulder. Mrdieel aid was sent for, and although Ken- drick's wound wee found to be a bad one, none of the in- jured persons are in a dangerous condition. No arrest has been made, and as the police have only a very vague des- cription of the man it is doubtful whether be will be I traced. ; I The Home Secretary has authorised the offer of a reward I of LIN) for informetion loading to the discovery antl convic- tion of the Men guilty of the attempted barglaly and shoot-

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN.—A Powerl'l" looking man, nulled John Wareing, was, on Monday., charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having been drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Bremner on Saturday night —From the evidence given, the prisoner seems to have made a most .determinect assault on the officer. Bre.mner, it Anne trcd, had been on duty 111 Eccles- ton-street about half-past seven on Saturday night, and seeing the prisoner drunk and behaving in a disorderly manner aslied him to go home. Wareing went into the Nag's Read publichonse, but was refused drink by the land lord owing to his being drunk. On coming put again he re- commenc d his disorderly conduct, and in consequence Bremner again accosted him. Wareing thereupon com- menced an assault, in which the officer was knockeil down and kicked and an attempt made by .he prisoner to choke him A. desperate strtugle then took place and lasted for about twenty minu i tes, and n the course of which the officer broke; his staff. On the appearance of two other officers, who had been told of what wls going on. Wareing was secured and lod i ged n the police office. Bremner's wrist was sprained in the encounter, and he had not been, able to be on duty over the week end. The prisoner said the officer used his staff so vigorously that his shirt was soaked with blood.. Superintendent Johnston said the PTISO- ner had been con v,cied on numerous occasions. Ie Was, in fact a very violent cliatkcter. Oa one occasion he ba& betn fined £5 and costs. Aind in defablti two months' impri- sonment, for an assault on a policeman. For the drunken- ness he was. fincti, I.os. and costs, and for the assault £5 and costs, or In default two months' imprisonment. —A rnala,.. named Adam Mason, was fiued ss. and costs for having beat. drunk and disorderly, and also ss. and costs for assaultir.g: P.C. STEALING ROPE.—On Thursday at Runcorn Police Court, Samuel Jones and John Wardle, boatmen, were each fined 20s and 203 costs, for having, on the 21st Wet, stolen 91bs of rope, the property of Isaac Jones, captain of the schooner Lady Neave. THE °UMBRAE OE SMALLPDX AT WIDNES.7—ALIOther out- break of this terrible disease as just occurred at Simms' Cross, thus bringing the total number of cases to five. The usual measures have teen taken to prevent the spread of the disease. A special meeting of the Health Committee of the Widnes Local Board ;vas held yesterday to consider the advisability of erecting an infectious hospital, but the pro- ceedings were private. OXFORD AND CAMBRIDGE EXAMINATION OF SCHOOLS.— SUCCESSFUL LOCAI, CANDIDATES.—The results of the Ox- ford and Cambridge examination of schools in various parts of the kingdom were issued at Oxford on Wednesday. The following are the names of the candidates in this neighbourhood who satisfied the examiners and obtained higher certificates :—E. A. Hutchison, Warrington Grammar School; C. S. 'Lackey, Warrington Grammar School. WIFE ASSAULT -A.T RUNCORN.—At the Runcorn Police Court on Tharday, a flatman named Thomas Weedall, of Bridgewater-street, was charged with assaulting his wife. On the 214 inst. Weedall was in a neighbour's house, when his wife threw a leaf at him through the window, lie then fol- lowed her up an entry, having a penknife in his hand, kicked her, and hit her several times in the face. She stated that her husband had beaten her several times before, and once flogged her with a rope.—Prisoner Was fined 403, and costs 12s di,

MANCHESTER Sims CANAL —A special meeting of the Provisional Committee was held in the Boardroom, Man- chester, on Tuesday afternoon; Mr. D. Adamson in the chair. A statement of receipts and expenditur4 to date, and also of assets and liabilities was submitted by the secretary, and, after a lengthened discussion, it wan resolved that a special meeting of the subscribers to the Parliamentary Fund be convened to be held in the Town Hall on Tuesday afternoon the 28th instant, for the purpose of receiving from th Provisional Committee a financial statement, and also for the purpose of conferring with a view to deciding as to the renewal of the application to Parliament next session. TRICYCLISTS' MEET AffD RACE AT RITNCORN.—A number of tricyclists met on Tuesday night at the Market-place, Runcorn, for a friendly run. They were accompanied by Mr. and Mrs. Mason, of Liverpool, two tricyclists who re- ently travelled a distance of 102 miles in 24- hours, be- sides a number of local bicyclists. The meet was the first held by the 'cyclists of the town, and it was a pronounced success. A pleasant run was made to Sutton Weaver, where a race was run on the Aston course in the presence of a number of spectators. Seven wheelmen entered the race, and a good start was efboted. from the usual point near to Sutton Weaver railway station. The course was and the comp,titora reached the goal as follows :--Itev. D. Llewellyn. 12mins. 16sec. ; C. Dauer', 20:nins. 30secs.; H. Salton, 20mins. 39secs. ; W. Brookes, 21inins. 153ecs ; Marsh and T. Taylor, 22mins. 303ecs. each; Horace Hand- ley, 23mins..30secs. ; Stevenson, 25m1ns. The riding was good throughout considering the condition of the road. Mr. C. Williams acted as starter and timekeeper. On returning from Sutton Weaver the riders at down to an excellent tea at Wilson's Hotel.

THE LONDON AND' NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY.—The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders cf the London and North—Western Railway Company, was held on Saturday, at the leuston Terminus. Mr. Richard Moon, the chairman, presided. In moving the adoption of the report, which re- commended dividerids.of 4 per cent. on the guaranteed and preference stock and 7 per cent on the consolidated stock, the chairman said the report was less satiefactory than any report that had been presented for some years, inasmuch as they bad had to trench upon the reserve fund, which now stood at £28,000. The expenses had increased 2.56 per cent. The expenses per train mile had been reduced by /d per mile, while the profit per traie mile was about id per mile less than it was a year ago. The parliamentary ex- penses had increased considerably, inasmuch as they had very importact bills to oppese. The principal one was the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which was probably one of the wildest schemes that ever entered into the minds of men, and interfered with their interests by dividing and diverting their railway, which they were bound to oppose. Referring to the Paesenger Duty Bill, Mr. Moon said that it had passed both Houses, and was waiting the lbsyal assent. What would be its effect upon them it was impossible to say ; but there was no doubt it effected them in all directiens, and required great consideration. Mr. Bancroft seconded the motion, and after some discussion, it was agreed to. CUTTING A MAN'S HEAD WITH A CAN.—James Rourke, We'sh's-yard, Old-raacl, Latchford, was charged on a warrant at Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, with assaulting Patrick Madonough.—Prosecutor had been helping to un- load a flat for Mr. Wall at Acton Grange on Sunday after- noon, and when they had nearly finished prisoner came on to the scene. The men who .had been working received a sovereign for their services, and they called at a publichouse and had a quart of lner, prisoner joining in drinking the beer although he had not been working. Prosecutor, pri- goner, and a man named Bourke, brother-in-law to the pri- soner, started for Warrington, and during the journey prisoner frequently asked prosecutor to lend him a shilling, but he refused to do so, saying he could not spare it. The three called at a beerhouse on Wilderspool-causeway and had more beer. When they were coming out of the house prisoner put his foot before prosecutor just when the latter was about to go down the steps, causing him to fall on his hinds and face. Prosecutor remonstrated with Bourke about allowing him to be treated in that manner, but he only received the sullen reply that "he might have lent the man a shilling." Prosecutor then decided to go home alone and proceeded along the river side. He had not gone far before prisoner, who had taken a can from Bourke, came up with him and struck a blow on the head with the can say- ing " Take that for your shilling." Blood began to spurt from his head, and he went to the police station and after- wards to the Infirmary, where the wound, which was an inch and a half in length, was stitched.—Prisoner was ordered to pay 20s. and costs or go to prison for a month. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COIL TRanEs.—There is a continued absence of any animation in the iron market, and on Tuesday there was not more than a moderate attendance on 'Change with very little inquiry. Trade, however, generally mainthins a steady tone. Makers are still kept tolerably well employed with the orders they have on their books and do not force business by reductions in price. On the other hand, the requirements of most of the large con- sumers are still, to a large extent, covered by deliveries under contract, and as there is evidently no apprehension of any upward movement in prices, buyers are quite In- different about placing out further orders until their re- quirements compel them to come into the market. In pig iron there is a small trade doing in a few orders given out to cover present wants. Local makers are firm at 455. to 45s 63., less 21- for forge and foundry qualities, delivered equal to Manchester, and in district brands quotations ie- remain on the basis of 45e. 4d. to 455. 103., less 2-.% for forge and foundry Lincolnshire delivered here. There is a moderate business doing in finished iron, and shipping in- quiries are coming forward rather more freely, chiefly for sheets for Russia and the Continent. Local manufacterers, generally, are fully employed, and prices remain at about £6 2s. 6d. to £6 55.; for ordinary bars, with better qualities, in some cases quoted at £6 7s. 63.; hoops, £6 121. 6(I. to £6 15s; and sheets, £8 to £3 7s. Gd. per ton, delivered into the Manchester district. In the coal trade there is a made- rate business being done and:in house fire coals there are in- dications that buying for winter requirements is already commencing. Common round coals move off fairly well, but engine fuel is still in moderate demand, with slack plentiful in the market, the wakes and holidays in the various manufacturing centres . and the present strike in the cotton trade having of course a tendency to restrict the con- sumption. Collieries generally throughout the district are running pretty near full time with comparatively only a a small quantity of coal going into stock, and the average prices at the pit mouth remain about as under : Best coal, 9s ; seconds, 7s ; common coal, 5s 6,1 to 6s ; bury. 4s 61 to 5s ; best slack, 3s 9d to 4s 33 ; and inferior sorts, 2s 9d to 3s 3d. As regards round coal, however, there is hardening tendency in the market, and there is every probability that some upward movement in prices will take place with the close of the month. In the Manchester district it is pro- bable that prices will be put up to the level at which they stood prior to the reduction in July, and in the ether dis- tricts advances of Gd to is per ton on round coal are talked of. The demand for-shipment continues good, and prices are steady'at 7s 3d to 7s 91 for steam coal, and 8s Gd to 8s -9d for seconds house coal delivered at Garston sr Liverpool.

JUVENILE TEMPLARY AT RUNCORN.—OD Saturday last, the quarterly meeting of the South-West Lancashire Dis- trict council held its first session in Runcorn. Besides the superintendent (Brother R. Anders, Liverpool) there were present representatives from the various temples in the dis- t ict. An increase of 40 members during the quarter was reported, the members now in good standing in the South- West Lane isliire District being 1900.. Brother D. Reid, D.T., Liverpool, and Brother Dooley (Balm of Gilead Tem- ple, Kensington), congratulated the district superintendent on the satisfactory report. Reports from 33 temples showed that the Order was steadily progressing. After tea a discus- sion took place with reference to the coming national prize competition. The district superintendents, Brothers Anders, Reid, and Hampson, congratulated the Runcorn Temple upon having obtained the first prize in. this district. In addition the prizes and certificates given by the Grand Lodge, the council intend in the future to offer extra inducements to those in this district. Brother Anders pre- sented Kate Heal with a first class certificate and prize, and Arthur Heal a second class certificate, which the council are having suitably framed. Mrs. Heal responded, and several members of the council addressed the juveniles pre- sent. A vote cf thanks to the Runcorn friends for the recep- tion given to the visitors closel the proceedings. LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE TELEPHONE EXCHANGE COMPANY.-At the annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Exchange Company, held at Man- chester, on Monday, Mr. Charles Moseley (chairman of the board of directors) presided, and there was a large attend- ance of subscribers. The annual report recorded that an increase had taken place in the business during the year to the extent of £12,000, the total income for the twelve months being £54,498, as against £42,817 last year. The balance of revenue account had, however, been very much reduced in cansequence of the losses entailed by the severe storm of December last, but the directors recommended a dividend of 5 per cent., and carried forward to next year the sum of £2,2o3.—The Chairman said they had made full and satis- factory arrangements with the Post Office authorities, and the Court of Appeal had decided that they were entitled to an absolute monopoly of the telephone for the remaining term of the patent within the district they sought to cover. With respect to Liverpool, there was doubtless a question in the minds of the subscribers there as to the efficiency of the , services in that city. It might appear as if there really was to be no settlement of this old standing matter, but he would , assure them that the removal oi a centre system such as ' they had in Liverpool abd the replacing it by a newer and better system was not very easily decided upon. In America they were divided as to the best system, and until it was settled which was the most efficient and economical centre I system, the directors had deferred settling the matter. In the meantime the subkct was receiving the very serious con- ' eideration of the board.—The report was adopted.

!THE SESSION DYING —MR. CROSS'S SPEECH ON THE INDIAN BUDGET—THE RESULTS OF THE SESSION—THE WAINWRIGHT BROTHERS—THE PARCELS POST—A PRINCE AMONG COOKS— THE poR r OF (")MMERCE—MR JOHN MORLEY'S NEW MAGAZINE—CAPTAIN WEBB'S COMRADE —MESSRS. AGNEW& PICTURE GALLERY. LONDON, THURSI)AY. The session dies bard, but its fate is now fixed to a minute. At two o'clock on Saturday Black Rod will knock at the closed door of the House of Commons and be- ing admitted will invite Mr. Speaker and members to attend in the other House and witnevs the prorogation by Royal Commission. It is a matter of usual occurrence that in the closing days of a session efforts should be made to cope with the accumulated amount of unfinished work. There are late sittings and even Saturday sittings, after which and just immediately preceding the prorogation comes a bill and the busy session dies quietly. That is a state of things varied this year. We have had every kind of unusual sittings. The House of Commons has sat not only on a Saturday, but has done a considerable stroke of business on a Sunday; whilst to complete the round of the week and fill in every possible 'interstice of time the House of Lords have met at four o'clock on a Wednesday and sat till a quarter to nine, thus grievously infringing upon the dinner hour.

One characteristic peculiarity of the session has been the statement on Indian finance three days:: before the actual ; prorogation. The Indian Budget is always late, but Ido I not remember when it was so late as this year. It was per- sonally a littic; hard on Mk Cross, who was left to deliver his great speech of the yea in the presence of something :liboa score of jaded gentlemen. In spite of this discourag- ing circumstance he achieved a genuine triumph, and justi- fied those anticipations of hit success which were widely and strongly entertained when the appointment was made. His speech was a master-piece of clear statement, showing ! a marvellous grasp of the multiplex details of Indian' fin- : ance. Mr. Matthew Arnold would have been greatly pleased with it, inasmuch as it possessed in high measure that great recommendation of lucidity, the comparative absence of which our great teacher has deplored.

Captain Webb has been buried at Oakwood Cemetery, not far from the scene of his gallant but hopeless enterprise. He is buried by the grave of a remarkable person, of whom holiday visitors to Niagara hear a great deal. He was called the Hermit of the Niagara, and a place where he was accustomed to bathe is to this thy cal led the Hermit's cascade. It is about sixty years since he first appeared on the scene, building himself a hut on one of the islands. He used to walk about on Goat Island as if it were Eel-pie Isle on the Thames, or some other eqtfilly unemotionable place. Of course, there was a mystery about him. He was said to be of high birth, self-exiled from England, because the fair I had proved false. This unhappy nobleman, after languish- . Img around the Falls for nearly tea years, was at last Idrowned while bathing in the pool of the cascade now I named after him. His body was recovered, and he sleeps I with his mystery in Oakwood Cemetery, now with Captain I Webb at his right hand. I No one who passes down Bond-street just now expects to see any cf the customary boards bearing announcements I that there are pictures being exhibited in almost every possible place. The services of those indefatigable public I personages, the " Sandwich-men," are quite at a discount, unless Perhaps there are a few left to announce that Dore's works are on view, a fact which by this time must be pretty generally known at the West Ead. Messrs. Agnew and Sons have not quite dismantled their walls at the Old Bond- street galleries, some excellent productions by foreign artists I of salon renowriPare to be seen there, and include Pierre Outin's "L'Emigrant," a picture illustrating a pathetic episode, as its title denotes ; two very natural bits of peasant life by Ariz, whose pictures are delightfully true to nature; and some very breezy coast scenes by Smith Hald. As usual some of the most popultr works in the Academy have retired to Messrs. Agnew's ; for instance Mr. Luke Fildee' "Village Wedding," and Mr. Frank Dicksee's not entirely satisfactoi y "Late Virgins."

The CLERK stated that at the time of the death of the late Mr. Twist, assistant overseer for Windle, there was a suns of £l2 17s 61 due to him. A cheque for the amount was drawn a few weeks ago payable to the. administrator of his estate, but after it was drawn he (the clerk) learned that Mr. Twist bad not made a will, and that the next of kin (his wife) had not taken out letters of administration. He asked the Local Government Board to authorise him to hand the money to Mrs. Twist so as to save the expense of administration, and the Board had written in reply that at the present stage they could not express an opinion upon the question. In the event of the sum referred to being paid to Mrs. Twist and charged in the Union accounts, it would rest with the auditor to decide in the first instance as to the legality of the charge, and the Board might hereafter give a decision.—The Clerk was instructed to retain the cheque until letters of administration were produced.

If anyone happens to be in want of a nok, a prince in his profession, I happen to know of one who is just now disengaged, cr will be disengaged at the end of this month. He is the chef of a member of the House of Commons, famous for his dinners, which go forward incessantly throughout the sesslon. The chef's salary is £2OO a year, at which, standing alone, he is regarded as cheap. But his employer was bound to take notice that, though he kept up ! an adequate establishment at his town house, he never gave a ! dinner, but he found charged to him extra attendants in the j kitchen each one paid at the rate of five shillings per dinner. i It was also Nought under his notice that these people were constantly changing. At the outside one came for half a !dozen times, then disappeared, and his or her place was taken by another. It was owing to some jealousy in the kitchen that the truth came out, and the nominal master of the house learned that the chef was in the habit of using his kitchen and its conveniences as a school of cookery. For some of his pupils he received as much as £5 a lesson; eneucrh oae might suppose to have enabled him to dispense with the extra five shillings which he charged his employer. It was this little bit of greed that ruined him, and now if anyone wants a thoroughly good cook on moderate terms 1 1 here's the man. •

Amongst the odd ways of getting a living whin% at sometimes disclosed is that of the commercial poet. He i a gentleman who will stoop from Parnassus to write you a verse or a poem on your business avocations. There was, about twenty years ago, a butterman in Liverpool who was understood to have made a large fortune through the efforts of his poet. The gifted man wrote every week a fresh poem about Kelly's butter, and all Liverpool thronged the store to taste the compound thus exto3lea. The other day one of these co-workers with Tennyson unhappily appeared at the police court, having somehow become unduly possessed of. money for which he had undertaken to give full value in poetry. He penned on a bold sc tie a poem which I think he called " London," the broad design being that a stranger supposed to be taking his walks abroad came in succession before the establishment of the poet's various customers, and was instantly struck with admiration at their quality and cheapness, admiration which he sought (,utlet for in some surprising verse. The Waverley pen is, through per- sistent advertisement, inalienably associated with a couplet. Probably it was the succ,!ss of the Waverley poet that sug- gested an application t.) Messrs. De la Roe for a commission to write something worthy of the growing popularity of the nti-stylographic pen in consideration of payment in ad- vance. Put Messrs. De la Rue have their own poet, and he, being "turned on," the following reply was despatched:—
It is Surely a loke, That you ask us ta buy A pi 6 in a p,ke. Of such bargains we're shy; In fact we must add, for ou don't seem to know It, That teddes making iieni we, keep our own poet.

The following report was presented to the Authority by the Frodsham Water Supply Committee :—The committee have carefully considered the terms and conditions re- quired for lands, easements, and water rights to carry out the Frodshara water echeme, as set out in Mr. Bancroft's report, dated 14th February, 1883, and in order to prevent any possibility of litigation in the matter they consider that provisional agreements should be entered into with Mrs. Hebbert, Mr. Heald, Mr. Wright, Mr. Wigginer, and Mr. Lewis. Your committee have negotiatedwith the above I parties and settled heads of provisional agreements in such ' form and upon such terms as your committee think will be in the interests cf the ratepayers, subject in each case to approval by the Authority and the sanction of the Local Government Board being obtained to the loan for proposed scheme. A detailed statement appended thereto, signed by Mr. Bancroft and marked "A," gives the gross total estimate cost of the scheme at £4,669 15s 61, but it should be explained that this sum is for the whole of the Broadley mill property may be die- posed of, reserving the water-rights which the authority ea- 1 quire, and without serious loss to the township. Your cemmittee, before arriving at the above resolution, caused a. house-to-house inspection to be made of those houses in the township of Frodsham Lordship, which could be supplied from the proposed melee, and the report of Mr. Farrington giving the result of such inspection is appended hereto marked" B," and in the opinion of the committee does not justify them in including the townehip of Frod- sham Lordship in the area of charged ; the cost of laying the mains in Frodshatn Lordship aed Button is, however, included in the seld total estimated cost of £4,769 15s Gd,and will doubtless result in a pecuinary gain for the township of Frodsham. A correspondent of a Liverpool contemporary says that in St. Helens, Widnes, and the adjacent manufacturing towns, where there is a tolerably well-paid working popula- tion, female gambling exists to a deplorable extent, the practice being carried on so openly and generally as to be almost as recognised an institution as the " public" itself. He describes its mode of operation thus Certain turf speculators issue weekly 'tickets' of the price of is or 6d el.ch, entitling the holders to a chance (!) of a prize; the value of the said prize varying with the original price of the ticket. These are issued in connection with nearly every 'event' of importance, so that the weekly supply is I exacqy maintained. The eagerness with which they are bought up by certain sections of the working class may be gathered from the fact that both • men and women regularly apportion sums varying from 61 to 4s per week tor the 'investment.' Many instances are recorded of money hav- ing been spent in 'tickets' whilst bare necessaries of life were wanting, and whilst shop scores ' stood at a formidable height. The immediate verdors of these tickets are certain publicans and tobacconists well known in the trade,' who are authorised agents of the turf speculators aforesaid. • One of these was recently located in Manchester, and did a roaring trade in this district. It is almost needless to remark that the investors 'have not the slightest guarantee that in appor- tioning tickets at the outset anything approaching to fair- ness is obeerved. 'rickets bearing numbers corresponding to the likely winners Can be sent to any town or district by the naanipulators. Of course, the more sensible and respectable of the working classes shun the systein, regard- ing it as a.transparent swindle. Female gambling of this kind nevertheless exists to an alarming extent, and any agitation for the suppression of the 'ticket' system would be deserving of the warmest public support,and if successful would confer a great boon upon thousands of workingmen and their wives."
