Ashton, Warburton, Camplan, Rigby, Smith, Whittaker, lii,zhfiald, Handley, Jackson, Weir, H. Linaher (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: Livsßroor. V MANCHESTER INFIRMARY,
div.p: Livsßroor. V MANCHESTER INFIRMARY,

A letter was read fm the Local Government Board asking what advantages would be derived from the payment of a subscription to the Liverpool Infirfnary.—Mr. %VET R thought it would have been better if the question had not been raised, and he moved that the motion in favour of paying a sub- scription, passed at the last meeting, be rescinded. Mr. RIGBY seconded the motion.—Mr; HANDLEY thought it w.fs a great pity to rescind the resolution, because it was really depriving half the population of the Union the advantages of infirmary treatment. Very few people went to Man- chester Infirmary, whereas that at Liverpool was easy of access. It was very inconvenient to go to Manchester. There was no direct train service from Runcorn, and it took something like thae hours to make the journey to Manches- ter, whereas only half an hour was taken up in the journey to Liverpool. Ile thought, seeing the small subscription required. it was better for the Board to subcribe to Liver- pool Infirmary, and do the greatest amount of good they possibly could, because there were many cases that needed infirmary treatment that did not get it because of the difiiculty in getting to Man- chester. The Board ought to consider as much as possible the wants, means, and convenience of the whole Union, rather than those of one section of it. From the .Runcorn side of the Union, which contained fully om-half of the entire population, Liverpool was more convenient than . Mancheser.—Mr. DARBYSIIIIIE said he would like to know if anyone had suffered through a subscription not being paid to the Liverpool Infirmary.—Mr. HANDLEY said there had been several cases which oaght to have been attended to at the Infirmary, hut the people had been the recipients ' of private charity.—Mr. RIGBY said he understood at the last meeting that a subscription of £5 53 to the Liverpool Ingrmary would not cover everything.—Mr. HANDLEY said washing and linen had to be plid for, but no doubt that would be provided by the friends.—Mr. RIGBY retnarked that the advantages did not seem to be any greater at Liver- pool than at Manchester, and he did not see why they should pay more than the .£3 3s. they now paid to Man- chester Infirmary.—After further consideration, the motion to rescind the previous resolution that a subscription be paid to Liverpool Infirmary was carried by six votes to four. THE UNION LUNATICS.

The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER reported as follows : Having been appointed as a deputation to visit the County Lunatic Asylum at Chester, we paid our visit or. Thursday. the 16th, accompanied by Dr. Robinson, medical racer of the workhouse, and Mr.Linaker, clerk to the Guardians. We arrived at the asylum at 1-45, and finished our work about 3-15. Thirty-one patients chargeable to the union were presented to us by Dr. Davidson, medical superinten- dent. Twenty of these were males and 11 females. They were questioned by us one by one, and we are sorry to re- port all the cases were hopeless. We found them clean and well cared for, and treated with the greatest kindness by the officials connected with the in,titution. The as ions ! has been much improved since our last visit, and the paint- ! ing and decoration of the different wards had a most cheer- ful appearance. Dr. Davidson and his assistaut Dr. Law- ranee treated us as usual very courteously. and showed and explained to us all the modern contrivances used in eases of lunacy.—The CLERK said during the many times he had visited the asylum he ILid never seen a more hopeless lot of lunatics than those the Board had there at the present time.

DECLINE OF VAGRANCY. The following report was read :—The committee having ' enquired into the wot king of the Vagrant Act, as applied to the admission to and discharge from the emu al wards of this workhouse report that, as compared with the seven months of 1882, January to June, there has been a great decrease in the number admitted. 1882: Admitted, 521; 1883: Do., 313, derease 208. Of these 313, 308 were dis- charged on the day following their admission, and 8 were detained for a period of more than one day. They recom- mend that (Ist) clauses 5,6, 7,9, and 12, of the Casual Poor Act, 1882, be printed and placed in a conspicuous position in the casual wards, (2nd) That the discretionary power hitherto exercised by the Master, under the authority of the Guardians, be continued. (3rd) That tht Master re- port to the Guardians at their next meeting following such discharge the names and reasons for the discharge of any casual poor discharged on the first day following their ad- mission, such rc.pot to Ise entered by the Master in the vagrant book. (4th) That the committee further engeire into the working of the Act in January, 1884.—The re- port was adopted on the motion ef Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. WEIR.

OUR. NATIONAL CHURCH. Sir,—llas an " Observer" read the whole of the corres- pondence on this matter? If he will do so carefully he will be able to answer his own qaery, " 'Why I attack Dis- ssnters ?" I cannot accept the statement of a " Visitor," because I am certain that unless he went right in the church he could not see how many people were in. And on inquiries let me tell him lam confirmed in my belief that such a state - of things never occurred. .But what was the curate's name, and when was the service? Now to Mr. Dix. I fail to find that he has replied to my challenge, or has supported in any way the statements he first made, and which I took up in my last letter. Indeed, his attempts at "explaining away" have been so nicely contrived that I fancy he must have bees studying Mr. Gladstone's epeaches to a very great extent. The funny and vague answer he makes as to orange lndaes, &re., is characteristic of the stamp of gentle- men to which I have an opinion Mr. Dix belongs. lam not going to express an opinion on the value or otherwise of Orangeism, but in fairness, and respecting the opinions of every man, I cannot bring myself to believe with Mr. Din that " Orangeism seems to exist for no other purpnse that that of perpetuating discoid and will amongst men claiming to have a monopoly cf Chris ian and social virtues." "An intolerant craving for supremacy characterises the ceremo- nial Churchman," he stays. If by this he means that Vas Church is still using evely endeavour to exercise her supremacy as the Parent Church, and also strenuous efforts to re gather her wayward children within her fold, I agree. " The. Church is stagnant," is the next statement he makes. IVtiat an assertion! Do facts support this? No. Since 1800, 9,000 churches have baen built, re-built, or restored ; the total cost of which can hardly be estimated, but it is computed that .C 34.000,000 was expended on church building and church restoration between 1840 and 1874, an amount which has since been increased to £4OOOOOOO. There were 5,947 parsonages in 1831 ; there are now over 11,000. Between 1841 and 1878 there has been an increase of 8,000 clergy, making a total something over 23,009. From 1839 , to August, 1877, the Church ra England subscribed for building Church schools £4,263,199, whilst the total sub- scriptions for British and foreign Wesleyan schools was £423.142, and for Roman Catholic schools £122,478. Again, the subscriptinns of Churchmen for 1877 was £620,034, against £104.930 subscribed by Dissenters. I could still go on with these figures, but I dare not trouble or trespiss on your kindness so far. And yet the " Church is stagnant." What have the clergy of the Church done for education? Listen here, Mr. Dix. Mr. Paxton Hood, Fate a Congregational minister in Manchcstsr who recently resigned his charge, and has gone to America, "driven forth," as he declares, by the deacons, says, " From whence came our best books? From whence did we obtain the the books which stirred, which taught—the books of criti- cism and exegesis—the books of the scholar, the poet, and I the novelist? Did they come from anv Dissenting coin- I munity at all; especially did they corns from theirs? Did I they not come from the Church of -England ?" As to the isolated Church census taking, I. have something more to- say. In the first place I am not going to admit the veracity of the reliability of any census taken by irresponsible news- paper proprietors or amateurs, for this reason, that the newspapers and the persons who take the censuses are, without scarcely an exception, of very strong bias against the Church. Does Mr. Dix recollect the census taken by Mr. Mill through the " Nonconformist " in 1872, and • which when overhauled was found to contain discrepancies of a most glaring character. Again, why are not the rural districts included ?- In order to prove the relative proportions of Church and Dissent the country , must be taken as a whole. The Church , I people have said for the last 30 years, I believe, that there should be an official census of the whole of England, and I believe that in the last Parliament an at- tempt was made to get a religious census clause inserted in- to the Census Act of 1881. But who opposed it ? The Liberationist members in the House of Commons. I con- tend myself that even supposing for one moment that the Church of England was in a minority, It is no argument against an Established Church. As my letter is likely to run out to a great length, may I have your permission, Mr. Editor, to break it here, with the intention of concluding it .n your next issue,—Yours truly, H. J. WESTBROOK.

Sir,—Will you permit- me to ask your correspondent " Dissenter " to name the" rates" which be paya. for the support of the National Church and whether he Mea2ll to convey by his letter that no workingmen in hie parish or neighbourhood are visited by Church of England•ruinisters ? If" Dissenter" does not wish to be so understood may I trouble him to say why he insinuates_ that a." drawing. room party" is necessary to secure the, clerical services. The reason "Dissenter" is not "called upon"' by Church of England ministers appears obvious. and I will venture to add justifiable. V. M. S.

PROVISIONAL MANSFERS.—At Prescot Petty. Sessions, on Tuesday, on the application of Mr. MacKenzie, a provisional transfer was obtained of the license of a baerhouse off Cyprus-street, Prescot, from John McDermott to Dick- son. Temporary authority was given to William rands to carry on the Engineer Inn, Sewell-street, Prescot, lately occupied by Henry Stuart.

- - A YOITTRFUL WANDERRIL—& lad, ag,d ten years, named Dtnel MeArdle, was on Friday charged at the St. fielens County Petty Sessions with having stolen a handkerchief contain:llg food belonging to William Burke. The prisoner, it seenied, belonged to Wigan, but was much addicted to wandering. On the morning previous he was seen to leave some pottery works at Eccleston with something under his ! coat. A youth ran after and caught him, when it was found that he was attempting to carry away Burke's dinner, Burke 'being one of the workmen.—It NW ordered that the prisoner should receive six strokes with a birch rod, and afterwards be sent off to Wigan. AN UNWILLING PROSECUTOR.—A young man named Agnes Kelly was on Saturday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having stolena jacket from the house of Catherine Lynch in Raglan-street. —Superintendent Johnson said the prosecutor Lynch gate information of the theft to the police, which she said had been committed by a young woman, answering to the description of the prisoner, who had lodged*with her a day or two. The prisoner was ap. prehencled, arid when Lynch fust saw her in the police office she said that she was the young woman referred to, but now A said that it was not her. On being put ipto the box lAnch said Kelly was not the young woman. 14 question. Kelly was in coasequnce discharited.

A trait of the Countess's pride is told in relation to one or two of these flowers, which no search could discover on her own domains, and which the artist-in-chief was solicit- ous to obtain elsewhere. The Countess in answer said,— " When I think of all I have got, I can but also reflect it is good to be reminded of what is denied to me. It is a salutory lesson, my friend. Leave it so." But it is to the larger of the compartments that our atten- tion is chiefly and perforce doe; the ones occupying the centre pf the panels, and displaying their wealth at the level of the eye. Thep are devoted to a series of exquisite paint- ings, lighly bat unerringly touched and tinted. completely illustrative of Milton's Pensereso. Did the lady who com- missioned these works long ago divine in her secret soul the sorrows of the future, and provide for them appropriate fowd in this sweet, sad work of Poet and Painter? Diu she e'en then feel a foretaste of to-day? • In this room she sits now, like a black statue amid these fair surroundings; motionless, except when touching, from time to time, through an acquired but unconscious habit, a magnificent ruby heart, eecrusted with diamonds, which she ever wears upon her breast in memory of a lost sister. Meanwhile her eyes are fixed upon the door, as if she half put to that the questions and momentous issue she is con- tinually repeating in theug,ht to herself concerning the doctor— "When will he come? Mitt will he say to ma?" Let me take the opportunity of the brief delay to try to describe her. The noble outline of feature and the dignity of personal bearing which we are accustomed to associate with high birth and breeding, and to a certain extent rightly, hut often very wrongly, are the first traits to arrest the eye as it lights on the Countess of Harlaxton. But even as one admires them they are soon over-looked or forgotten altogether in still more interesting features, that are so subtle in themselves, and so liable to change and melt one into another, as to perplex an observer who tries to mne to any settled conclusions. The softness and playfal mobility of the mood of one hour or day, the ten- derness and fixed melancholy of that of the nett, are at times so impressive as to melee it difficult afterwards to realise the strong will, the unchaiging purpose, discover- ebbs in the set of the delicately eirvent Mouth ; or the irritable pride that at the first suspicion of offence expands the nostril, and erects and sends back the head in haughty suspense to wait for explanation or apology. Time has dealt with her in capricious fashion, has turned her once, heautious brown hair to silvery white, for- getting she is yet but fifty six; and made the thin, pale

kNiViitATlot4 OF CaILDREN TO CANADA, Mr. HARTLEY stated that since last meeting 27 children, whem it was proposed to send to Canada, had attended at Prescot Police Court before two justices sitting in petty sessions, and signified their consent to their removal to Canada. The Local Government Board asked that a formal resolution to the following effect should be passed and transmitted to them, along with the magistrates' certificate: —" That the several parsons hereunder mentioned being desirous of emigrating to Canada, the necessary steps be immediately taken to effect the emigration, and that a sum not exceeding £lO be expended for each person, and charged to the com:non fund of the Union." The names of the intending emigrants were appended to the resolution.— On the motion of Mr. NEWSOME, seconded by the Rev. J. BARNACLE, the resolution was agreed to.—Mr. NEWSuME said the proposed conductor was a clergyman recommended by Father Nugent.

A DISORDERLY CCSTOMER.—At the Warrington OCCA- sional Court House, on Monday, before Mr. Greenall, Martin Cassidy was charged with being drunk and disor- derly and creating a disturbance, at the Millstone Inn, on the previous evening. It was gated that prisoner had smashed a pane of glass in the door, and also broken a winclew.—He was fined 53. and costs. THE WEA.TIIER.—The charming and beautiful weather daring the pres-nt week has realty been a boon and a bles- sing to the farmers. From morning to night the sun has shone almost uninterrupted:y, and the grain and other crops have been rapidly ripened for the harvest. Harvest operations are in full swing on cvery hand, and there is every prospect of a rich and bountiful in-gathering. THE ROBBERY AT NEWTON BRIDGE RAILWAY STATION. —lt will be remembered that about two months ago John Johnson, a young man residing in Gas-street, Crow-lane, was fined 20s. and costs for breaking into Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son's bookstall at Newton Bridge station, and stealing therefrom two books and several packs of cards. He was allowed the opportunity of paying the fine' but as he has not done so, he was on Monday evening last appre- hended, and committed to prison for one month in default. TEE PRINT WORKS TRIP Iro LIVERPOOL —The annual excursion in connection with the printing works of Messrs. McCorquodale and Co., Newton, took place on Saturday,the destination as in former years, being Liverpool. The popu- larity of the trip was as marked as ever,and upwards of 1,600 persons proceeded by it. In addition to these many hundreds of other persons visited the famous seaport, the day fortu- nately being remarkably fine for an outing. It is a pleasure to learn Rut everything passed off without mishap or acci- dent, and praise is due to the railway officials forthe manner in which they discharged their duties on the pressing occa- sion. .EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLAIIS —The usual weekly meet- ing of the members of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Tempters was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening last, Brother Henry Warburton, W.C.T., presiding. There Was a good attendance. One new mem- bar was initiated and two proposed. After the transaction of the formal business, the meeting of the District Lodge to be held to-morrow (Saturday) afternoon, was fully discussed and several arraegements made in connection therewith. A digest of the proposed business was read, and the lodge representatives were instructed thereon. The night's pro- gramme was.headed A night with the Poets," and a goodly number of the members gave selections, which were both appropriately chosen and excellently given. A very plea- sant evening was spent. PAPER ON "A TRIP TO BLACKPOOL."—A meeting and entertainment in connection with the Baptist Band of Hope and Temperance Society was held in the Baptist School. Earleetown, on Tueeday evening, when there was a very good attendance. The Rev, W. C. Taylor presided. The early portion of the gathering was occupied by the members of the juvenile associetien, who ove an excellent selection -of recitttions, songs, ke3., which were much appreciated. Subsequently Mr. Multens read an interesting paper on " A trip to Blackpool "—a narration of his day's out at the popular seaside resort mentioned. He explained that he proceeded by one of the special trains arranged in connec- tion with the Viaduct Works excursion, and arrived at his destination shortly after nine o'clock. He alluded to the throng of those anxious to find him accommodation, or pro- vide him with breakfast, and afterwards went on to give a deecrintion of his day's wanderings. He visited the Aquarium, the Winter Gardens, Raikes Hall Gardens, and also had the pleasure and gratification of hearing the well-known Swiss Alpine Choir, the performance by whom he characterised as the ,st beautiful and splendid he ever heard. Regardless of the occasional heavy downpour of rain he thoroughly en- joyed himeelf during the day, and came home refreshed and ready to resume his day's labour. The paper was listened to with a considerab!e degree of interest, and was sup- plemented by Mr. Adams, who briefly narrated his experience during a recent excursion to Belle Vue Gardens, Manchester. He said he always found that wbere the whisky bottle was absent everything was peaceful and quiet, but where the whisky bottle was "flying about" there was ne peace either for those who used it or those in the neighbourhood. - The meeting then concluded.
A girl of fifteen, Annie Dowle by name, is unkbir remand at Greenwich accused of hurglariously entering a house in Lower Sydenham and stealing a silver watch and other articles.

ASHTON. ANOTHER PRESENTATION TO THE ASHTON CHURCH AtSOCIATION.—On Tuesday afternoon last the committee of the Cave-Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane. Ashton, received a gift of about 250 books and pamphlets from the Council of the Church Association in London. The works are on various subjects related to the teachings and prin- ciples of the Church Association, and the handsome gift has been received with gratitude by the committee. They form an agreeable addition to the Sunday School Library. A RUNAWAY HORSE: SHOCKING ACCIDENT.—A sad and serious accident was the result of a horse, belonging to Messrs. Crippin, of Bryn Hall, taking fright on Sunday morning last. The animal, attached to a milk cart, was standing in the farm yard, and, from some cause, suddenly bolted along the road in the direction of Ashton. Singular to say, the horse proceeded along the route usually taken in the daily milk round, and whilst it was dashing along Gerard • street a young man, named Andrew O'Brien, attempted to stop it. He ran in front and held up his arms, but he was knocked down by the horse, and being run overr he sustained very severe and dangerous injuries. He was picked up and conveyed to the' surgery of Dr. Hannah, and that gentleman immediately dressed the wound One of the wheals had passed over the young man's head, and had cut and mutilated his scalp in almost numberless places, some of the wounds being two, three, and nearly six inches in length, while his right ear was cut clear away with the exception of a piece of skin at the bottom. The poor fellow was subsequentlAconveyed to the Wigan Infirmary, where he at present remains. ACrION AGAINST THE POLICE FOR FALSE IMPRISON- MENT AND DAMA,GES.—Before Mr. Flonlkes, at the Wigan County Court, on Wedneslay, James Hill, an organist, of Crook, Pemberton, brought an action against P.S. Sayers, RC. Jackson, and P.C. Joss, of Pemberton, to recover the sum of £5O for alleged false imprisonment on the 17th April last.—lt appears that on tha date named, about half- past eleven o'clock 'at night, the plaintiff was dthing home from Ashton to Pemberton. When at Goose Green be was met by the three officers, who considered him incapable of taking care of the horse and trap, and charged him with being drunk and asleep therein. He was ultimately locked up after a struggle, and the case was subsequently heard at the Wigan County Police Court, when it was dismissed. Hill now brought the present action to recover damages against the police. He was represented by Mr. Lees (solicitor), while Mr. Ellis appeared for the police. Mr. Hill, Mr. Winiam Melling (landlord of the King's Arms, Ashton), Mary Ann Melling (daughter of Mr. Melling), James Vernon (Ashton), and another witness, gave evidence to the effect that Hill was not drunk when he left the king's Arms, Ashton, to return home about eleven o'clock at night. —The case was not completed when the court rose, and it was adjourned. DINNER TO THE ASHTON YEOMANRY TROOPS: PRESEN- TATIONS.—Upwards of 60 members of the "A " (Ashton- in-Makerfield) troop of the Lancashire Hussars Yeomanry Orvalry sat down to an excellent dinner at the Gerard's Arms Hotel, Ashton, on Saturday evening last. Amongst the officers and invited guests present were Major Reif (ex- adjutant of the corps), Quirtermaster-Sergeant Livesley, Sergeant-Major Healy, Mr. W. Balharry, Mr. W. Melling, and Mr. Ferguson. After the wants of the "inner man " had been supplied, Major Reif presided, and Quartermister- Sergeant Livesley occupied the vice-chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were duly honoured, after which a very interesting ceremony took place. This consisted in the pre- sentation to Sergeant Long and Private James Caunce (Haydock) of marks of the esteem of their fellow-troopers on their retirement after periods of long and creditable service. The presentations were made in accordance with the rules of the "Troops fund "—oat of which the costs of the gifts are defrayed. Sergeant Long has been associated with the "A " troop for no less than 30 years, and he was presented with a hand- some black marble timepiece; whilst Private Caunce, who had served 24 years, was given a valuable silver watch and guard. Major Reif made the presentations on behalf of the traop, and in doing to spoke highly of the two recipients. The gifts were suitably acknowledged. The proceedings throughout were of a very pleasant and enjoyable char- acter.

A WASTHEL.—At Wigan, on Monday, the maOstrates committed a man named John Goulding to prison for three months for ar. assault on his wife, and granted the latter a protection order and an allowance of 53. a week. The pri- soner was Said to be a drunken, idle fellow, who constantly assaulted his wife. He had been married 14 years, and during that time had not given her £l4.

FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' ANNIVERSARIES AT CULCEIETII. The anniversary of the Union Friendly Society was held at the Pack Horse Inn, Newchurch, Culchetb, on Saturday afternoon. The members met at one o'clock, and about three o'clock they sat down to an excellent dinner, provided by Miss Lowe, the land,.ndy, after which they formed a procession and, headed by the Lowton Brass Band, paraded the village, and visited the residence of Dr. Sepliton and others. Sabeequently dancing was heartily engaged in until closing time. The band played a choice selection of music ' during the afternoon in a highly creditable manner, under the conductorship of Mr. TbOMAS Booth, the bandmaster. It appears the society numbers 76 members, with funds to the amount of £652 16e 2d. Mr. Isaac Unsworth is the secretary.—The members of the St. Peter's Glory Court, No. 941, of the Ancient Order of Foresters held their anni- versary at the New Inn, Calcheth, also on Saturday. The members began to assemble about one o'clock, and at three they sat down to a substantial dinner, provided by Mr. and Mrs. Low, the host and hostess, after which a procession was formed and, headed by the Glazebury Brass Band, paraded the village, visiting the residences of Dr. Sephton, Mr. James, Culcheth Hall, and others during the march. The members wore green favours, which added greatly to their appearance. The band played an excellent selection of music during the evening, under the conductorship of Mr. Richard Collier, and dancing was heartily engaged in until about 11 o'clock, when the proceedings terminated. FRODSHAM. PICNIC TO FRODSIIA3I.—On Saturday the employes oi Messrs. J. O'Neill and Co., upholsterers, cabinet makers, &c., of 16, Church-street, Liverpool, had their annual picnic at Overton Hills. At 11-30 the emplov6s, numbering up- wards of 80, left Lime-street station in first class carriages en route for Frodsham. On arriving the party indulged in a variety of sports, and at four o'clock sat down to a sump- tuous repast, Mr. F. J. Gardner, a member of the firm, pre- siding. Before the party returned home three cheers were called for the respective partners, and responded to in the most hearty manner, which must have been most gratifying to the firm. It was admitted by each one that a most en- joyable day had been spent, and all returned to their res- pective homes well pleased with their visit to Frodsham. The whole of the arrangements were carried out by Mr. W. , Kerr, to whom great credit is due. EDUCATIONAL WORK AT FRODSIIAII.—A meeting of the Frodsham Local School Attendance Committee was held in the girls' school, Frodsham, on Monday evening, at seven o'clock, and the committee sat until half-past ten investigat- ing the various cases. The extraordinary length of the meeting will be understood when it is stated that 85 parents in respect of 126 children attended the meeting, and 23 others sent messengers or letters in respect of 28 children. Eleven parents of 14 children neither attended or sent any word of explanation. At the same meeting Mr. Thomas Riley, school attendance officer, presented a complete census of all children residing in Frodsham and Frodsham Lord- ship between the ages of three and thirteen years, from which it appeared that the tot number of children was 900, and classified as follows, viz : between the ages of three and four. 108; feur and five, 108; five and six, 78; six and seven, 105; seven and eight, 93; eight and nine, 90; nine and ten, 85; ten and eleven, 82; eleven and twelve, 71 ; twelve and thirteen, 75 ; total, 900. Of the above 900 enumerated children 623 were attending certified efficient schools, 83 children were attending private schools or being educated at home, 146 were not attending any school but were under school age, 10 children had passed the required standard, 17 children i'ere suffering from physical or mental ailments, and 21 children were ab- sent from school without any reasonable excuse, but two of these children were only residing temporarily in the dis- trict. Mr. Riley stated in his report that with regard te the census generally he believed it to be nearly accurate, if not quite as regards the number of children between the ages of 3 and 13, but the ages of some children 'might not be quite correct, as many of the parents were either unable or un- willing to give the exact age, but with some corrections made since he considered it fairly reliable. A BOY DROWNED AT LYMII.-An inquest was held at the Police Court, Lyman, on Tuesday, by Mr. T. J. Ridg- way, coroner, relative to the death of Thomas Wilson' nine years of age, son of Thomas Wilson, fustian cutter, Rush -Green. The evidence showed that on Monday John Clare, six years of age, was walking near the canal in the direc- tion of Rush Green, when he saw the deceased playing with a piece of bark which was in the canal. lie was trying to reach the bark, and fell into the water.-Joseph Badieley, a lad employed at Higher L ; c.:s returning in his cart from tieatley station, and had reached the Dog Bridge, when he saw something in the water. He could just see deceased's bead, and c ailed out to a lad behind him to get assistance. He could not render assistance himself, as he had his horse with him, and had been forbidden by his master to go away from it.-Mrs. Owen and Mrs. Horsefield, who live a short distance away came to the canal, and made efforts to save the lad who, however, sank just before Mr. Forster, one of the jury who, attracted by screams, came up. The body was recovered by a boatman. The Coroner bad . received a letter Irvin the Rev. Nit% Cullin, suLivezing that a life buoy be placed at or near Oughtrington Bridge. People were continually attracted by barges and steamers, and all their efforts did not suffice to prevent occasional immersions. The Coroner observed that seine two or three years ago a jury made a similar recommendation, and a life buoy was hung up somewhere on the canal bank. Me did net know whether it had been of service yet or not. Sergeant Harrington remarked that it was instrumental in saving a drowning man who fell into the water some time ago in the dark. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned. DEATH OF THE COMTE DE CHAMBORD.—A Central News telegram from Frohsdorf states that the Comte de Cham- berd died at six o'clock yesterday morning,af ter a prolonged struggle. A GOVERNMENT STEAMER SUNK—The Goveenment steamer Tbarnee collided with the steamer Egypt, off Wol- wich Arsenal, yesterday morning. The Thames, which was much damaged, afterwards sank. THE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN WALE 3. Four deaths have up to the present occurred from the recent explosion at the Geld Pit, and several of the injured are in a precarious stare. The pit is being reworked, but the shifts are not fully constituted. SCENE AT A FIRE.—A fire occurred early yesterday morning in a dwelling-house at Stratford, Essex. The oc- cupant, named Green, with his six children and a lady lodger, were aroused and rescued in their night shirts, es- caping with some burns and bruises. A BENEVOLENT LADY.—Mrs. Love, widow of a coal owner, died yesterday at Durham, aged 83. Since the death of her hveleand, eight years since, she had given away £50,000 in religious and philanthropic objects, the Metho- dist New Connection being the chief recipients. THE FRENCH AMBASSADOR.—The Press Association learns that M. Waddington, the French Ambaesador, left London unexpecredly yesterday morning for Paris. It is not known whether his Excellency will return before Mon- day, when he was expected to go for a two months' leave. BREAKING A MAN'S LEG.—At Preston, yesterday, Daniel Matthews, a bailiff, was charged with unlawfully wounding John Barker, another bailiff. It is alleged that the prisoner took a run kick at Barker, breaking his leg. The prosecutor lies in a dangerous condition and his depositions have been taken. The prisoner was reminded. PAYING DE—Messrs. Le May, hop factors, last night gave a complimentary dinner, at Tunbridge Wells, to the creditors of their old estate, numbering about 80. Each gentleman received the balance of the amount lost when the firm stopped payment five years since. The toast of the tion was enthusiastically received. THE LATE DR. MOFFAT.—A Very natural sequence of of the death of the late Dr. Robert Moffat is that a move ment has been started for the erection of a memorial. The scope of the project has not yet been determined, but it will probably take the form of a nionument ver the gra tt rnis• sionary's grave, and perhaps a tablet or bust in Weetmineter Abbey. PRIZ,L FIGHT NEAR BIRMINGHAM —On Thursday a large numb. r of thr pugilistic fraternity asseinleed at Aston, a suburb of Birmingham, and two men, named Jecksen amid Dingly, had a tight for £lO a side. The combatants fought stubbornly for upwards of twenty minutes, when J.,ckson was declared the winner. Speculation was carried on briskly, and some hundreds of pounds passed bends. SINGING IN PUBLIC-HOUSES.—At the annual licensing meeting field at Dudley, yesterday, a memorial signed by 1,100 inhabitants was presented to the magistrates urging that musical accompaniments to singing in taverns should be allowed. The bench refused to accede to the reqte,s's of the memorialists with a view of deci-easing drunkenness. Boer ACCIDENT: SEVEN Lives Losr.—lnfornaltion re- ceived yesterday morning from Lloyd's states that the learqut. Voyager, of Banff, homeward 'bound from the West Indies to England, is lying at Berracq lino, waiting to get to sea. The captain, two of the crew, and four men from the shore went out in the ship's launch to sound the her, but nothing his since been braid of them, and it is con- sidered certain that they have all been drowned. THE DAPHNE DISASTER: CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION.— At the Glasgow Sheriff's Court, yesterday,Mrs. Rose Carbery, of Armagh, sued Messrs. Stephen, ship builders, for one thousand pounds compensation for the loss of her son by the Daphne clieaster. The deceased earned Hs 9d weekly. Defendants contended the claim was excessive. Mrs. Cal bury intends to move for change of trial to the Court of Session, that the case may be tried before a jury. IMPENDING COLLAPSE OF THE NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE STRIKE.—.I he North Staffordshire miniois' strike is rapidly coining to an end. The three largest concerns in the dis- trict are now in full work, and no inconvenience is being experienced in cons( (pence of the mere handful of men still remaining out. Workmen are applying at Earl Granvillte's at the rate eif between 30 and 40 a day, while Messrs. Robt. Reath and Sun, having their full complement, are daily re- fusing proffered labour. RAILWAY COLLISION AT RETFORD.—S/lOrtly after eleven o'clock yesterday morning, as a passenger train from Lin- coln was approaching Retford station, on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, it came into collision with a goods train standing at the east end signal box, striking the rear part of the train with great violence. The goods van and one of the waggons were literally broken to fragments, other waggons and the engine being daineged. The line was I:locked for over two hours. No one appears to have been injured. A MAN KICKED TO DEATH AT BIRMINGHAM.—A resp•e:- table man named John Dukes, of Tower-street. Birmingham, died late on Thursday night at the Queen's Hospital from the effects of terrible injuries inflicted by a gang of roughs who attacked him in Hill-street, a much-frequented thor,aghfare in the centre of the town. The deceased had changed a sovereign at the General Elliott Hotel, and it is supposed that someone in the bar had observed this and followed him out. He had not proceeded far when he was attacked from behind, thrown violently to the ground, and held down by the throat while his pockets were being rifl something being placed ovel• his mouth to prevent his screaming. Having taken his money from him, the rufli ens kicked the deceased about the head, knocking out several of his teeth, fracturing his skull, and leaving him insensible upon the ground. No arrests have yet been made. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS. The Apprcbation Bill was read a third time and passed. —On consideration of the Commons reasons for disagreeing with the Lords ainendments to the Agricultural Holdings (England) Bill Lord CARLINGFORD moved that their lord- ships do not insist on the amendment.—The Marquis of SALISBURY defended the amendment; but would not divide -against motion. After discussion it was agreed the Lords do not iist on the amendment. The amendment to_ the scotch Agricultural Holdings Bill was also not insisted ou.—The House adjourned at ten to five.

FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE.—Cases of foot-and-mouth disease have occurred on premises belonging to Thomas Shovelton, Bedford, Leigh; Francis Bradshaw, Chaddock- lane, Tyldesley ; and Robert R. Wright, Newton Hall, Newton.

CHESHIRE FARMERS AND THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS BILL.—On Saturday afternoon, at a meeting of the Chester Farmers' Club, the Agricutural Holdings Bill was discussed at length, and eventually the following resolution was carried without dissentients :—" That the members of this club protest against the way in which the Tenants' Com- pensation Bill has been despoiled of some of its best pro- visions, particularly by the House of Lords, and hopes the Ministry will not accept the amendments." PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD —The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Monday evening. Mr. C. Spenceley pre- 'sided, and there were also present Messrs. J. T. Hall, W. Goldsworth, Sandets, T. P. Hewitt, and H. Cross (clerk ). The Board were occupied upwards of two hours diecuseing in private a report by H.M. Inspector of Schools. On the motion of Mr. Sanders, seconded by Mr. Uoldsworth, Mr. Henry. Hall was appointed a teacher in the boys' school at a salary of £4O a year.—The inspector's report was considered exceedingly unsatisfactory. The Board having received the explanations of the principal teachers in reference to it, a long discussion took pl iCP, and it was resolved to retain the services of the existing staff for another 12 months, they undertaking to put in practice the recommendations and suggestions contained in the inspector's report, and to increase the Government grant a 3 much as possible.

- - THE FEVER OUTBREAK AT SANDRACH GOVERNMENT IFQIIIRY.-Mr. Smith, C.E., an inspector under the Local Government Board, conducted an inquiry at Bandbach, on Wednesday, with respect to a complaint made by a number of the principal inhabitants that the Local Board had made default in providing sewerage and waterworks, in removing refuse, and other matters affecting the sanitary condition of the town.—Mr. R. Bygett appeared for the complainants, and the Rev. J. R. armitsted (the vicar of the parish) ap- peared for the 1 ocal Board, of which he is chairman.—The Board admitted being in default as regards sewerage works. There was no effective drainage at all in several parts of the town.—The medical officer of the town (Dr. Fox) said that fever existed in nearly every street, and there had been several deaths already. He feared that a clearance of the infantile population such as took place in 1878, would recur.—Dr. Carter Bell testified that the quality of the water taken from the various pumps and wells of the town was on the whole highly dangerona.—Mr. Bancroft, engineer, Manchester, stated that a supply of water might be had at a reasonable cost.—The defence of the Board was that the ratepayers had shown themselves to be utterly opposed to public waterworks.—The Inspector, however, remarked that the Public Health Act did not say a word about the wishes of the ratepayers.—lt is now understood that the Board will be compelled to conform to the Act or be a Board in default.

SOUTHWORTiI- WITH-CROFT SOLITHWORTH-WITH-CROFT SCHOOL BOUM:I.—The monthly meeting of this board was held at the Beard school on Tues- day evening. Present—the Rev. T. P. Kirkman (chairman 1 and clerk), and Messrs James Hatton, Lewis Birchall, Richard Turner, and Alfred Dixon (s,chool attendance officer). The attendance officer submitted the names of several children in irregular attendance at the schools in the district, and he :vas instructed to again warn their parents that unless their children attended school more regularly they would be summoned before the magistrates. It was unanimowdy resolved that the board spend £3 in provisions for the annual children's treat, to be held on the Bth Sep- tember next, and that the treat be carried out under the management of the School Board and churchwardens as in previous years. Several accoants having been passed, the proceedings terminated.

_ WINSFORD. CLUB ANNIVERSARIES.—ne anniversary of the "Vale Royal" Ancient Order of Foresters was celebrated on Sat- urday last, when, as usual, the members walked through the streets headed by the Rifle band, An excellent dinner was provided for them at the Red Lion, Over. The club is in a flourishing condition, as is also the Ancient Order of Shepherds, Over, who also held their anniversary. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, STATION-ROAD.— The Sunday school anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday afternoon and evening, by Mr. R. H. Pole, of Northwich. In the morning the teachers and scholars pro- cessioned the streets, when suitable addresses were given and hymns sung. A tea meeting was held on Monday, which was well attended, and it was followed by an address to parents and children by Mr. R. H. Poole entitled "Beware of Dogs." SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS.—The annual sermons in con- nection with the Weaver Navigation Church, Winsford, were preached on Sunday. The Rev. E. Nixon, M.A., preached in the morning; in the afternoon a children's service was held; and in the evening the Rev. E. C. Reid, M.A , rector of Church Coppenhall, Crewe, preached to a crowded con- eregation from ‘• Speak Lord, for Thy servant heareth." The sermon was characterised throughout by a thrilling el quence and enchanced the attention of the -congregation from beginning to end. The service was choral, .and collec- tions were made at the close of each sermon. s. d. s. d. THE CHESTER PARLIAMENTARY IMPROVEMENT BILL.— The voting papers were distributed to the ratepayers of Cheer On Thursday morning, and will be collected on Monday next. _

CHESTER MAGISTRATES AND REFRESHMENT LICENSES FOR THE AUTUMN SPORTS —Application was made by 11 persons before Sir Thomas Frost, mayor of Chestar, on Wednesday, for special licenses for the sale of refreshments on the Roodee on Wednesday next, the occasion being tbe autumn sports.—The Chief-Constable called attention to the act which provided that magistrates could only grant licenses which would "conduce to public convenience, comfort, and order."—Mr. Stevenson, of the Blossoms Hotel, pleaded that a license in his case would condocs to public convenience and comfort.—The magistrates retired, and, on returning to court, the Mayor said: We do not agree as to the desirability of- granting these licenses, and intend to call all the magistrates together on Saturday morning to give a , final decision in reference to these applications.

PROPOSALS TO INCORPORATE WINSFORD.—The ratepayers of Winstead, Cheshire, on Wednesday night passed a reso- lution in favour of applying to the Privy Council in com- mon with Over for a joint charter of incorporation. The Cheater magistrates have committed for trial a man named Robert Jones, who is charged with haying attempted to naurder his child, first by beating it; head against a tele- graph post, and then throwing the child into the canal. The prisoner had been drinking heavily. RAVAGES OF INSECT PEST IN CHESHlRE.—Generally throughout Cheshire, mangolds have been entirely des- troyed by insect pests. The losses to farmers will be severe. The insects attacked the young plants as soon as they ap- peared, and whole fields are barren. Fortunately for fodder purposes for much and fat stock during winter, turnips are above an average crop. Patatoes are an abundant and healthy crop. CATTLE DISEASE IN CHESHlRE.—Chesbire farmers are strongly complaining of the introduction of cattle disease into their districts by aninuls brought from Ireland, which are sent over without proper veterinary examination. Amongst a herd of Irish cattle received at Crewe last week, one was suffering from disease, and immediately slaughtered. Afterwards the disease broke out among others that had been sold and moved into other districts. OUTRAGES ON IRISH HARVESTMEN IN CHESIIIRE.—De- spite the fact that attention has been called in the House of Commons to outrages on Irish harvestmen in Cheshire, it is stated that another man has been seized and kicked by Englishmen in a most brutal fashion. Summonses have been made returnable for Monday next. -By means of threats and violence Irish harvestmen have been entirely cleared out from a large district in Cheshire.

CATTLE DISEASE IN 'CHESHIRE : PROHIBITION AGAINST limn CATTLE.—The Cheshire magistrates hastily con- vened on Wednesday night, at Crewe, to consider an out- break of disease among a herd of Irish cattle in Crewe, struck a heavy blow against the great fair and abattoirs recently established by a private company at Crewe Station, Nvith the powerful assistance of the London and North-Western Railway Co. After prolonged discussion they decided that foot-and-mouth disease being so prevalent in Ireland at present it was necessary to absolutely pro- hibit the importation of Irish ctttle into Cheshire, as being toe best means of ridding the county of the disease. •

CHESHIRE lIIINT PUPPY Snow.—The judging' of the puppies which have been " walked " by Cheshire farmers has taken place at the Forest Kennels, the judges being Mr. Castlemau, huntsman of the Atherstone-; Mr. C. Ludharn, huntsman of the Meynell ; and Mr. Dickens, Luntsman of the North Staffordshire. The first prize for dogs was given to Mr. J. Merton Hall, of Budwortb, for Leader. Mr. Walter Tynsley took second with Lipman; and Mrs. Rigby, of Kingsley, third with Stranger. Mr. Tynsley gave up the second prize, and it was passed, on to Mrs. Rigby. The third prize was then awarded• to Mr. Tickle, of Aston,' Northwich, for Link Boy. The fisrt prize for bitches was gained by Mrs. Darlinelon. of Ice, with Virulent; the second by Mr. Hassall, also of Ince, with Victoria; aud the third by Mr. Norcross, of Kingsley, with Gay Lass. From all parts of Cheshire reports come that foxe3 are very numerous, and an excellent season is expected. PROPOSA: TO CLOSE ALL PUBLIC-HOUSES IN CREWE.— At the Brewster Licensing Sessions, at Crewe, on Tuesday, the Rev. A. W. Potts and a number of ministers of the town attended as a deputation to present a memorial asking the magistrates "in the full and unfettered discretion which the law gives them over any and all licenses (eteept grocers), to suppress these sources of poverty, disease, and crime, by refusing to renew every license in the borough, whether on or off."—The Rev. Mr. Potts said be was aware that there was a technical objection to this proposal, inas- much as they had not given the usual seven days' notice; but he asked the magistrates, with a view to the reduction of tne licenses, to adjourn seme of them to the next sessions in order that notice might be given.—Tne Bench refired to consider, and on their return the Mayor (who is a prominent member of the Blue Ribbon Army) announced that all the existing licenses would be renewed with the exception of two, against the holders cf which the police had made an objection. These would be adjourned till the next atesions.
